experiences.title: EdgeVerve Interview Experience | On-Campus Recruitment
experiences.full_content:
The on-campus recruitment process for the Product Development Associate (PDA) role at EdgeVerve was well-structured and thorough, assessing both technical expertise and interpersonal skills. The process comprised three key rounds: a technical assessment, a technical interview, and an HR interview. Here’s a detailed overview of my journey.

Round 1: Technical Assessment

The first round was an online coding test focused on Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA). It included three coding problems with varying levels of difficulty:

Key Topics Covered:

1. Array manipulations

Dynamic programming
Graphs and trees
String algorithms
2. Duration: 3 hours

This round required strong problem-solving skills and the ability to write optimized, efficient code. Familiarity with common DSA patterns was critical to performing well.

Round 2: Technical Interview

The second round was a one-on-one technical interview, which evaluated both project knowledge and DSA skills.

1. Project Discussion

The interviewer asked in-depth questions about the projects I listed in my resume. Key areas included:

The problem the project aimed to solve.
My specific contributions and responsibilities.
Tools, technologies, and frameworks used.
Challenges faced and how I addressed them.
Clear and confident communication about the project’s workflow, implementation, and impact was vital.

2. DSA Questions

In addition to project discussions, I was given two to three DSA problems (easy to medium difficulty) to solve during the interview. Tasks included:

Solving problems on the spot.
Explaining my thought process and approach.
Writing and optimizing code in real-time.
Preparation Tips: Practicing mock interviews and revising common algorithms helped me navigate this round successfully.

Round 3: HR Interview

The final round focused on assessing my behavioral skills, career aspirations, and fit within the organization.

1. Behavioral Questions:

The HR asked situational questions to understand my problem-solving approach, teamwork, and motivation. Examples included:

“Tell me about a time you faced a challenge and how you overcame it.”
“How do you handle conflicts in a team?”
“What motivates you to perform well at work?”

2. Feasibility and Availability:

This segment assessed my adaptability to organizational demands and long-term career goals. Common questions were:

“Are you comfortable with relocating?”
“What are your career aspirations?”
“How do you see yourself contributing to EdgeVerve?”
Tips for Success: Show clarity about your goals, align them with the company’s vision, and maintain professionalism throughout.

Conclusion

The EdgeVerve recruitment process was a comprehensive evaluation of technical proficiency, interpersonal skills, and adaptability. Each round was designed to test specific competencies, making it both challenging and enriching.

For anyone aspiring to join EdgeVerve or similar organizations, my advice is:

Build a strong foundation in DSA and project development.
Be thorough with your resume and prepared to explain your projects.
Practice behavioral questions to improve communication and align your goals with the company’s values.
The journey may be rigorous, but it’s a rewarding experience that sharpens both technical and soft skills.

experiences.title: Educational Initiatives Interview Experience | Software Developer Full Time
experiences.full_content:
I recently went through the interview process for the role of Software Developer at Educational Initiatives. The selection journey was comprehensive, involving multiple stages designed to evaluate technical expertise, problem-solving skills, and adaptability. Here’s a detailed breakdown of my experience, from the initial project submission to the final HR interview.

Initial Screening

Candidates were tasked with completing two projects within a week. The projects focused on software design patterns and OOP concepts, with preferred languages being Java, C#, and TypeScript. I chose Java for my implementation.

At the end of the week, during the pre-placement talk, the results of the initial screening were announced.

Technical Interview 1

Duration: 1 hour

This round began with questions based on my resume, covering topics such as my projects, domain of interest, and specific skills.

Code Walkthrough and Enhancements

1. I was asked to dry-run my code and explain the rationale behind incorporating specific features and design patterns.

Tip: Highlight exception handling, design patterns, and adherence to SOLID principles in your code.

2. Additional challenges were posed to improve the existing code. For instance, I was asked to:

Encrypt and decrypt satellite commands using the RSA algorithm.
Implement periodic logging of satellite status after every five commands.
Tip: You’ll have 30–45 minutes to implement such features. Delivering clean and executable code ahead of time earns extra points.

DSA and Algorithm Questions

Find the factorial of a number.
Discuss various sorting algorithms and their time complexities.
Evaluate mathematical expressions.
Tip: Avoid solutions with high time complexities (e.g., O(N^2) or O(N!)). If your logic is sound, you may skip writing pseudo-code.

SQL Queries

If DBMS is mentioned in your resume, expect medium-to-hard SQL queries. Since I didn’t include SQL in my resume, I was only asked basic queries.

Tip: Mention SQL in your resume only if you’re confident in your skills.

Technical Interview 2

Duration: 20–40 minutes

This round’s focus depended on feedback from the first interviewer. It could be either highly technical or similar to a managerial round. Questions included:

Basic DSA problems.
Topics from the resume, such as skills and projects.

Final HR Interview

Duration: 30 minutes

This round was more relaxed and conversational.

The CTO started by asking about my code, followed by general questions from my resume.
The HR inquired about my relocation preferences and asked questions to assess my adaptability and communication skills.
Tip: Be casual, calm, and articulate your thoughts clearly. The goal is to showcase your ability to adapt to new teams and environments.

Key Takeaways

Demonstrate a solid understanding of design patterns, SOLID principles, and DSA.
Be prepared to implement new features or optimize your existing code under time constraints.
Tailor your resume to include skills you’re confident in, especially for SQL or DBMS.
Stay calm and confident throughout the process, especially in the HR round.
The overall process tested technical expertise, problem-solving skills, and adaptability, providing a great learning experience.

experiences.full_content:
EmbedUR visited our campus in the month of November , hiring for Software Engineers. It offered a CTC of 8 LPA , with a 3 years employment bond and other multiple opportunities for package upgradation.

About EmbedUR

EmbedUR is basically a software development company specialized in making embedded systems with focus on AI & ML. In the JD for software developers they mentioned C programming would be an advantage.

Round 1 ( Online Assessment ) -

Around 2000 students from our college were shortlisted for giving the test. The test was taken on their own testing platform. The comprised of Aptitude , Logical  Reasoning , Pseudocodes , C Programming [ In depth knowledge ] , Microprocessor and Microcontroller Concepts [ 8051 , 8085 , etc ] (focus on their architectures).

Round 2 ( Technical Group Discussion 1 ) -

Around 600 people were shortlisted from the OA for this round. Batches of 10-12 students were made and were sent to the GD rooms , where one interviewer would be present. The interviewer would be asking questions and whoever knows the answer can raise their hands and answer the question. Their was no individual questioning.

The questions I faced were -

1. Difference between a process and a thread

2. CCMA and collision detection and avoidance in Computer Networks

3. AVL Trees and their balancing factors , different rotations of the tree.

4. Inter-process Communications

5. Traversals in Doubly Linked List

Moreover , the questions were mostly from the domain of the degree that majority of the students were pursuing in the group.

Round 3 (Technical Group Discussion 2) -

For this round , 57 people were selected out of 600. Here also groups of 10 students were made. In this round , although it was mentioned as GD , but inside the room every student was asked a particular set of questions individually.

The questions that I faced were -

1. Difference between ML & DL

2. Explain one ML Algorithm that I found Interestion

3. What is double pointer in CPP

4. Difference between Microcontroller and Microprocessor

5. OOPS Concept in Java

Round 4 ( Technical + Managerial Round ) -

30 were shortlisted for this round.

It was a face to face interview with 3 panel members [ One from Engineering Team , One from Management and another from HR ]

I was asked about my self introduction followed by Linux , how it is better than Windows , command to list all the running processes , fork() function , Stack Pointer and Instruction Pointer , my primary coding language ,  What if I am assigned a role that is not from my current degree, my family background , If I am willing to relocate.

Round 5 ( Final HR Round for Selected Candidates ) -

8 people were called for this round and final discussions about the offer were made.

experiences.title: Energy Exemplar Interview Experience | On-Campus  | Associate Software Engineer | Internship + FTE
experiences.full_content:
Round 1: Technical and Project Assessment (30-45 min)

Brief Introduction

In the first round, I was asked to solve a DSA question involving the creation of an N-ary tree, as well as performing BFS and DFS traversal on it. Following that, the interviewer asked me about some basic OOP concepts and dynamic memory allocation.

Next, I was asked to describe my project, including its features and usage. The interviewer then reviewed my GitHub and LinkedIn profiles, during which he inquired about my internship experience. The round concluded with a few basic Git commands.

Round 2: Development and Project Assessment (~1 hour)

Brief Introduction

This round was entirely focused on development and was quite challenging. The interviewer noted every keyword I mentioned during my introduction and asked follow-up questions about each one. He also inquired about my specific contributions during my internship.

The interviewer then questioned me on every technology stack listed in my resume, probing into the internal workings of the packages I used. For instance, in my case, he asked about Hive, BLOC, Firebase, and the Razorpay payment gateway.

Following that, I was asked some straightforward System Design and DBMS questions, like the role of a load balancer and the concepts of vertical and horizontal scaling. Instead of asking for direct definitions, the interviewer presented a scenario where a virtual machine is deployed on a server with millions of incoming requests and asked how I would handle it.

Later, he asked me to create the database schema for one of my full-stack projects and then convert a one-to-many relationship into a many-to-many relationship.

Other topics covered included:

Normalization and its forms
Docker/Containerization
Linear Merge vs. Squash Merge in Git
Authorization vs. Authentication
Caching
JWT (JSON Web Token)
All the questions were based on the technologies mentioned in my resume, so it's crucial to have a deep understanding of everything you include. Many questions were situational, requiring me to solve problems rather than just provide definitions.

Round 3: Vice President (~45 min)

Brief Introduction

The final round began with questions about my internship experience. Then, I was given a DSA question to detect a loop in a singly linked list, with a follow-up question to find the starting point of the loop.

The interviewer also asked me about the parameters used to evaluate the efficiency of a sorting algorithm. He then asked me to write and explain four sorting algorithms, including Quick Sort.

For all the coding tasks, I had to write the code syntactically correctly on paper.

After some time, I was called to the HR round, where I received the offer.

Best of Luck!

I hope you all land your dream job.

Warm regards,

Nitin Chandra Sahu (https://www.linkedin.com/in/nitinchandrasahu)

experiences.title: Entrata India Interview Experience | Software Engineer | Full Time
experiences.full_content:
I recently had the opportunity to interview for a position at Entrata Pune, a leading provider of property management software. The process involved two rounds, covering OOP, DBMS, DSA, and project-based questions. Here’s a detailed breakdown of my experience:

Round 1: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) and Database Management Systems (DBMS)

Introduction and Online Assessment Question:

Discussed my solution to a basic string problem from the Striver A2Z sheet.
Compared the use of LinkedLists vs Vector/Array, explaining the advantages of each data structure.

ER Diagram to Tables:

Converted a given ER diagram into tables and wrote corresponding SQL queries.

Conceptual Questions:

Difference between RDBMS and DBMS.
Wrote SQL queries involving JOIN and aggregation functions.

OOP Concepts:

Listed the pillars of OOP and explained inheritance with its types.
Wrote code demonstrating multilevel inheritance.

Round 2: Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA), Project, and HR Questions

Project Discussion:

Explained my SIH team project, which was a MERN Stack-based application.

Motivational Question:

Answered why I wanted to join Entrata Pune.

Website Optimization:

Discussed methods to reduce website loading time and increase refresh rate.
Identified causes of high loading time and proposed optimization strategies.

DSA Questions:

Explained Dijkstra's Algorithm, wrote the code on paper, and provided the syntax for the priority queue used in the solution.
Discussed matrix implementation logic.

Game Logic:

Developed logic/pseudocode for a Snake and Ladder-style game.

Verdict

Selected

Conclusion

The interview process at Entrata Pune tested a mix of technical, problem-solving, and communication skills. The focus on core subjects like OOP, DBMS, and DSA, along with project-based discussions, made it a challenging yet rewarding experience.

experiences.full_content:
Eucloid Campus Recruitment Experience

Eucloid visited our campus for recruitment for the first time, conducting the entire process virtually. The recruitment journey began with a presentation, followed by an online test, and concluded with interviews on the following day.

Round 1: Online Test

The first round consisted of an online assessment featuring multiple-choice questions aimed at evaluating candidates’ analytical thinking, logical reasoning, and problem-solving skills. The topics covered included:

Aptitude
Mathematics
Statistics
Verbal Ability
Puzzles
Notably, there were no coding questions in this round.

Out of the 99 students who participated in the assessment, 42 were shortlisted for the technical interview. Although there was a slight delay in announcing the results, the placement cell communicated the outcomes around 11 AM the following day.

Round 2: Technical Interview

The technical interview was conducted via Microsoft Teams and began with a self-introduction. The interviewer then asked me to discuss my web development projects, specifically one that I had highlighted on my resume. I utilized the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) method to effectively explain the project, particularly focusing on my use of AWS for deployment.

Key Questions Asked:

What is a Data Engineer?
Can you explain the Star Schema?
How would you rate yourself in SQL on a scale of 1 to 10?
What is the difference between Drop and Truncate?
What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING clauses?
Which window function is used to access the value in the next row?
I correctly identified the LEAD function and elaborated on its boundary conditions. The interviewer then posed additional questions regarding window functions, including the differences between RANK and DENSE_RANK.

Next, I was asked about my problem-solving skills and to tackle the following puzzles:

Water Jug Problem
8 Balls Puzzle
Cake Cutting Puzzle
I successfully provided solutions to all puzzles and explained my approach. The interviewer maintained a professional and courteous demeanor throughout the session, concluding by asking if I had any questions. I inquired about areas for improvement, and he responded positively, indicating he was fully satisfied with my performance.

In total, 13 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

Round 3: Interview with the Leadership Team (Technical and HR)

This round was conducted by the Director of Data Engineering. He began by inquiring about my previous interview experience before delving into questions about my project.

He expressed particular interest in my cloud experience, prompting me to share my screen and explain both the code and the user interface of my project, including an in-depth explanation of the Sequelize ORM used in my backend.

The Director asked about my technical decisions, and I elaborated on each feature in detail. Additionally, he inquired about my experience as a domain director for my college clubs, as mentioned on my resume.

The session concluded with another puzzle: the Man Fell in the Well Puzzle.

Conclusion

At the end of the recruitment process, five candidates received offers, and I was thrilled to be one of them. This experience not only sharpened my technical skills but also improved my ability to communicate effectively about my work.

experiences.title: EY Interview Experience
experiences.full_content:
On August 21st, 2024, I had the opportunity to interview with EY for a consultant role during their recruitment drive at Sister Nivedita University. The process was both insightful and challenging, consisting of four rounds, with around 300 students shortlisted after the first two rounds.

Round 1: Aptitude Test

The first round focused on basic aptitude questions, covering topics such as OOPs, DSA, OS, and reasoning. Additionally, there were two coding questions—one based on strings and the other on arrays—both of easy to moderate difficulty.

Round 2: English Versant Test

In this round, I used a Bluetooth microphone to respond to various types of questions, which included reading comprehension, listening comprehension, repeating words, and correcting grammatical errors.

Round 3: Technical Interview

After a long wait (my interview, scheduled for 9:00 a.m., wasn’t conducted until 4:00 p.m.), I finally had my technical interview.

Topics Covered: My project, specifically the user authentication system built with Express.js and bcrypt, along with questions on cybersecurity.
Challenges: While I could answer questions about my project, I wasn’t fully prepared for the cybersecurity questions.

Round 4: HR Round

Unfortunately, I did not make it to the HR round. However, I realized the importance of being thoroughly prepared for both the technical aspects of your projects and broader topics like cybersecurity, even if they don’t seem directly relevant. It's also crucial to be well-versed in core concepts like OOPs and SQL, as many of my peers were asked about these.

Outcome:

Of the 300 students interviewed, 67 were selected for the consultant role, which came with a salary package of 4.8 LPA. While I wasn’t selected, I gained valuable experience and insight into the process. This on-campus opportunity was organized by my college, which is affiliated with MAKAUT. Though I wasn’t successful this time, I remain determined and hopeful for better results in the future.

experiences.title: EY GDS  Interview Experience | On Campus recruitment | Tech Consultant | 2024
experiences.full_content:
I am a B.Tech fresher, and I recently had the opportunity to interview for the Consultant role at EY GDS. Here’s a detailed breakdown of my recruitment process to help fellow aspirants prepare effectively.

Recruitment Process Rounds

1. Online Assessment

The first stage was an online test, which included:

Aptitude Section: Questions on logical reasoning, quantitative aptitude, and verbal ability.
Coding Section: A single coding problem of easy difficulty. Candidates were given 45 minutes to solve it.
Preparation Tip: Practice aptitude questions using YouTube resources and solve coding problems on platforms like GeeksforGeeks and LeetCode.

2. Verbal Ability Test

This online round assessed listening and speaking skills, focusing on verbal communication.

3. Technical Interview

The technical round was an in-depth assessment of my:

Core Technical Concepts: Focus on Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs), its real-life applications, and core principles. Since my preferred language is Java, many Java-specific questions were asked, which aligned with the interviewer’s expertise.
Project Discussion: Questions about my academic projects, their implementation, and challenges faced.
Database Concepts: Topics like Joins, Normalization, and one SQL query.
Coding: Two coding questions related to HashMap and HashSet.

4. HR Interview

The HR round was conversational and relatively easy. Topics included:

Personal Background: Family details and reasons for choosing Java as my primary programming language.
Technological Trends: Questions on upcoming technologies.
Role Understanding: Differences between the work of a Developer and a Consultant.
Puzzle Question: A simple problem-solving question to gauge analytical thinking.

Result

Out of 120 students interviewed from my college, 22 were selected, and I am thrilled to be among them.

Closing Note

For all aspirants aiming for such roles, focus on building strong foundational knowledge, practicing problem-solving, and understanding the role-specific requirements. All the best!

experiences.full_content:
Round 1:

Online Assessment on the SHL Platform:

- English Comprehension: 22 Questions in 18 minutes

- Logical Ability: 14 Questions in 14 minutes

- Quantitative Ability: 14 Questions in 20 minutes

- Automata (Coding): 2 Questions in 45 minutes (Very Easy: e.g., Sum of digits; sum of digits that are prime numbers, etc.). You only need to write the function.

- SVAR Conversational - Spoken English: 7 sections

- Section 1: Listen and repeat the sentence.

- Section 2: Repeat the sentence by filling in the missing word.

- Section 3: Listen to a conversation and answer questions verbally.

- Section 4: Repeat the sentence by correcting errors.

- Section 5: You'll be given a topic with 30 seconds of prep time, then you need to speak on it for 45 seconds.

(I don’t remember the other two sections.)

You need to be quick and efficient. In some colleges, the assessment and the spoken English parts took place on different days, but for us, they were on the same day, within the same assessment. The questions are easy, but switching between sections or even between questions within the same section is not allowed. The time provided is the total time for the section, not per question, but be mindful of your time. Also, you can switch back and forth between the two coding questions.

They took almost a week to declare the results of the assessment; only 30% were selected. Be fast, and ensure no one else is detected on your camera. On our campus, they divided everyone into various roles (criteria unknown, perhaps lexicographically or by stream). Categories included BPM, FS IT Control, GRC Technology, Non-FS Risk Transformation, Oracle/EA, Cyber, Non-FS TRPM. It’s a good idea to review the core competency you're allotted before the interview.

Round 2: Technical In-Person Interview

The interviewer started with small talk like how I was and then asked me:

- "Where do you see yourself in 5 years?" (Be diplomatic with your answer.)

- Tell me about yourself.

- Real-world application of your project.

- What are joins in SQL?

- Identify primary and foreign keys.

- What's the difference between the two?

- Difference between inner join and outer join.

- Left join, right join.

- Gave three easy SQL queries to write involving joins.

- What is recursion? Benefits of recursion.

- Write code for Fibonacci using recursion.

- What’s the edge case? When will the loop stop?

- Difference between a singly linked list and a doubly linked list; advantages of DLL over SLL.

- What is a tree data structure? What's the last node of the tree called?

- What is binary search? Explain.

- Do you know machine learning (ML)?

I said yes, so he asked:

- What is regression?

- Do you have any experience in ML?

I said yes, I had built a project, so he asked me to explain it.

- Gave me a puzzle: YouTube Link

- Do you have any questions for me?

I asked two questions: one about the solution to the puzzle (he smiled and said, "Good question") and another about the kind of projects freshers are expected to work on after joining. He answered both in detail.

Kept the resume [Tip: Take two copies of your resume].

I got shortlisted for the HR Round.

Round 3 - HR Round:

- Tell me about yourself.

- Job location preference.

- What do you know about EY's work culture?

- What's your hometown?

- Family background; about your parents.

- What did you learn in your B.Tech, and how will it help you work better at EY?

The interviewer said, "The interview is over, and you can go."

After all this, I was rejected. Result declaration took about a week.

If you’re still here after all this, here are some observations and advice; you can take it or leave it:

1. Be fast and accurate in the online assessment. Ensure no one is within your camera’s range, and that your phone doesn’t appear in the camera during the online assessment. This is the stage where many deserving candidates got eliminated.

2. Some people were only asked situational questions, while others (like me) faced full-fledged technical questions. If you’re shortlisted for a less tech-focused role, expect situational questions.

3. Be diplomatic when answering "Where do you see yourself in 5/10 years?" Don’t give them the impression that you’re too ambitious, as this might work against you.

4. If you are unable to answer some technical questions, that's okay too. In fact, don't be an idiot and jump enthusiastically at every question they ask you, like me. Show them you are struggling and willing to learn, even if you remember questions like Fibonacci, even using DP, like the back of your hand. Your chances of getting shortlisted are higher if you let a question or two slide and remain confident in your communication.

5. Speak confidently, smile often, and be humble.

6. And if you still get rejected… I don’t have any specific advice for that. Rejections are tough. Process it in your own way (get a big tub of ice cream, or curl up in your hostel bed and skip dinner for the day—it’s okay). But no matter what, get back up and keep going ;)

experiences.title: Facilio Interview Experience | Software Engineer | Full Time
experiences.full_content:
Hello everyone! I’d like to share my journey through the Facilio campus placement process during my final year in Computer Science Engineering (CSE). Facilio visited my college for campus recruitment, and I was fortunate to participate. Here’s a detailed breakdown of my experience:

First Round: Aptitude and Basic Programming

The first round consisted of two parts: aptitude and basic programming. The questions tested general reasoning skills as well as fundamental programming knowledge. I was able to clear this round successfully and move on to the next stage.

Second Round: Problem-Solving

The second round took place at the Facilio office and was focused on problem-solving. We were given six problems to solve within three hours, with difficulty levels ranging from basic to medium and hard. The problems were similar to those found on coding platforms like GeeksforGeeks and LeetCode. I managed to solve five out of the six problems, which felt like a great achievement.

Following this round, Facilio’s team shortlisted candidates for the final interview, and I was thrilled to see my name on the list.

Final Round: Interview

The final round was an interview that covered Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) concepts, data structures, and problem-solving based on the questions from the second round. I gave it my best shot, but unfortunately, I wasn't selected in the end.

Conclusion

Although I didn't make it through, the entire experience was incredibly valuable. The process was challenging, and the environment at Facilio was fantastic. It was a great learning opportunity, and I thoroughly enjoyed every step of the recruitment journey.

experiences.full_content:
Greetings, everyone!

I am Vanshika Rathod currently pursuing MTech. integrated course from IIPS-DAVV, Indore (2020-2025) , I am here to share my incredible interview experience with you all

I had the privilege of participating in the recruitment process at my college, where FICO offered three roles this time namely Software Development , Solution Engineer and Quality Assurance Roles.

After resume shortlisting ,nearly 500 to 550 students had the privilege to give the online test and out of them only 39 aced it to the Interview round. My journey through the FICO interview process consisted of six rounds, yes that's what it took us to join a pioneering and reputed company like FICO , I’d like to take you through each of them.

Round 1 : (Coding Round)

In this round, there were a total of 18 questions, comprising 2 coding questions focused on Data Structures and Algorithms, and the remaining 16 were multiple-choice questions. The test had a duration of 90 minutes and was conducted on the Code-Signal platform, with no negative marking.

MCQ Section: The MCQ section included 16 questions, each carrying 5 marks/points. Approximately 6-7 questions were centered around Logical Reasoning and Quantitative Aptitude, while the remaining 6-7 questions were related to Computer Science fundamentals. The Computer Science questions covered various topics, including Object-Oriented Programming , Java output-based questions, and Design Patterns.

Coding Question: There were 2 coding questions in this round, both of medium to hard difficulty level, points 200 and 400 respectively .It was mandatory to code in java  ,thus it is advised to candidates to be well-prepared to code in Java, otherwise they might end up losing the round just due to the language preferences. Even I faced this restriction due to my preference to code in C++.

After the online test, results were out within a day and to our surprise many of  those were not selected who could not solve both the coding questions and so only around 39 students only made it to the next round in contrast to last year when 132 students had successfully received the interview invitations , I felt fortunate to be among those shortlisted, and it was an exciting opportunity.

Round 2: (Technical Interview)

Each of us who were shortlisted had different panelists, in my case interview duration was about 30mins (max) the interview was conducted on Zoom at 12 noon, 2nd August.

Interviewer/Panelist: Sandhya Ma'am

(NOTE : She was very humble and supportive throughout the interview period because I was nervous due to certain technical glitch on my side ,if any such problem occurs, just drink some water and hold a warm smile)

Technical – Round 1 Questions:

Tell me about yourself
Basic discussion on project, Technologies/libraries and basic functionalities used to make it?
Asked me to rate in JavaScript ,cpp java, since they were mentioned on my resume skills section
What is package in java, how are they defined and used/code syntax?
What are classes, types of classes in java?
Describe class vs object.
What are constructors and it's types in java?
Elaborate on any 2 Pillars of oops.
What is Jar file ?
Familiarity with C++ language, DBMS? (She was testing if really know the things I have mentioned so far)
Lastly , she asked me if I had any queries.
I wasn’t asked much  about  DSA problem because she might have visited LeetCode profile during my interview and be impressed by it, since I had solved about 500+ problems which I think is remarkable enough to leave an impression. So personally I suggest having a good coding profile as it does matter in the Interview.

After a day we got the results , around half of the interviewees were accepted for the next round, however this time strangely many of the students were added in the final list for next round ,mostly those holding 8+ CGPA. Henceforth it is advised to not overlook CGPA , because the harsh reality is CGPA matters a lot in placements. So an important tip would be to manage getting a decent CGPA of 8.5+ since it helps a lot ,I have personally witnessed this

Key tips to crack interviews : Maintain good eye contact, display confidence, overcome the fear of rejection, give your best effort, make the most of your time, wear appropriate attire, and showcase your dedication and enthusiasm.

Round 3: GD-Group Discussion Round (Offline- 5th August)

NOTE: The rule to crack this round is that there are no rules, because our strategies failed to work  but keep calm and keep interacting throughout to increase your chances of getting selected.

All of us were asked of divided into two groups  about 15 students in each group.

There were 2 topics :-

Topic 1: Social Networking: Pros and Cons
Topic 2: AI in HealthCare: Pros and Cons
Step 1: Open Discussion

Step 2: Half of the group were made to speak for the motion and the others were made to speak against the motion.

Step 3: Roles were swapped i.e. those who spoke for the motion were made to speak against the topic and vice-versa.

Step 4: 20seconds conclusion from every one individually.

Result was out immediately after a lot of anticipation and nervousness we were informed that only around 24 out of 34 students were privileged to sit in the subsequent round.

Tips for GD:  Be a team player, listen actively, initiate the discussion, be concise, participate  enthusiastically.

To give further details the process was not the usual HR round but the next round quite unexpectedly was a System Design copy-pen test , Henceforth it is highly advised to delve into all the technical subjects including System Design.

Round 4: System Design (Offline/pen-paper)

TOPIC: Topic was centered around the current affairs in trend i.e. Olympics ,So the topic given was "Medal Tally System"

This round comprised of designing all the three of below mentioned design within a fixed time bound of 15mins only:

Conceptual Design (5 mins)
Low-Level Design (5 mins)
High-Level Design (5 mins)
Result: About 18 of us proceeded to the next round, this was quite unexpected round for us .

Although this time it was quite new to us, it is advised to be thorough with system design fundamentals.

Round 5: Technical Round 2:

Many of  us including me were asked only managerial questions only since I had already faced an interview round earlier but many of us were asked about the technical concepts and DSA too who came direct in the GD round.

Questions:

What did you eat today?
Where do you stay?
Will it be comfortable for you to relocate to Bangalore?
What do you feel about Indore ,favorite food here?
What do you like doing in spare time?
What kind of a person you are?
What do your friends tell about you?
Why 8.91 CGPA not 9+?
What do you think whether you are a hardworking or intelligent?
Family Background?
Ratings and proficiency in programming languages
About  the course, is it integrated course?
Any questions?
Simultaneously HR round was also going on and only few of  us were sent to the HR Round.

Round 6: HR Round

Are you suitable for Bangalore location?
Any plans of Higher Studies?
Family Background
Discussion on preferred role and flexibility for other roles.
Any questions/queries.
Verdict : SELECTED

I was elated to be informed that I was among the 9 selects who got selected, roles were also immediately assigned to us after suspenseful wait of 10 to 20 minutes, the results got disclosed.

The entire process was a roller-coaster of emotions, I would like to thank someone who was continuous source of motivation and guidance to me. Looking forward to starting a new chapter of my life.

I hope my experience inspires and encourages fellow students to persevere and never lose hope, no matter how challenging the journey may be. Thank you for listening to my interview experience!

experiences.title: Fidelity Investments Interview Experience for Apprenticeship
experiences.full_content:
Hi all,
I hope you are doing well!

First of all, I would like to wish "All the best" to those who are preparing for MNC company interviews. Today, I’m going to share my interview experience for the apprenticeship role at Fidelity Investments.

I first applied for the role through the Naukri portal, and about a week later, I received an exam invitation from the Fidelity admin team. I registered using the provided exam link and began the interview process.

Round 1: Online Assessment

The assessment covered English grammar, basic aptitude, and core computer science concepts such as OOP, data structures and algorithms, computer networks, and Python and C++ (MCQ questions). After completing this section, I moved on to the coding section, which included one coding problem. You are given sufficient time to solve the problem, with a focus primarily on array and string concepts. Following the coding section, there is a final section where you are asked to write an algorithm for a given question, mostly focusing on DSA-type algorithms. This section was the easiest; as long as you understand the concept, you can write the algorithm in your own words.

Round 2: Telephonic Interview

After completing the online assessment, I received a call from one of the team members at Fidelity a week later. They informed me that I had passed the assessment, collected my personal details, and explained the interview process. The team member mentioned that I would receive an email regarding the technical round in a couple of weeks.

Round 3: Technical Round

I received an email inviting me to a technical round, which was conducted via Zoom. The technical HR introduced himself, mentioned his role, and asked me to introduce myself. He inquired about my degree, final year projects, internships, and technical skills as listed on my resume. He went through my resume in detail, and I gave my best responses.

Round 4: HR Round

After the technical round, I received a call informing me that I had cleared it and that my HR round would be held on the same day. I was prepared and ready to attend. The HR round was also conducted via Zoom. The HR arrived on time, introduced himself, and discussed the company's activities, as well as the roles and responsibilities for the apprenticeship position. He then asked me to introduce myself and inquired about my projects, internships, and my school and college life. Afterward, he congratulated me, saying I was selected for the role and that I would receive further details via email. I thanked him for the opportunity.

Verdict: SELECTED
Difficulty: Intermediate

experiences.title: Finzly Interview Experience | Trainee Software Engineer | Off-Campus
experiences.full_content:
My Interview Experience with Finzly

In November-December 2023, I reached out to Finzly’s HR via LinkedIn, but I didn’t receive a response. However, in June 2024, I finally got a reply from HR, and they sent me a test link on the Coderbyte platform. The test comprised two coding questions—one easy and one medium—along with 30 aptitude questions and a few open-ended, non-technical questions. I successfully completed both coding questions, passing all the test cases.

A week after submitting the test, I followed up with HR and received an invitation for the first technical interview. This interview was conducted online. The interviewer was very friendly and supportive. The topics covered included three DSA questions (two easy and one medium) and a few SQL queries related to DBMS. The main focus was on Java, as the company primarily works with Java, and it was highlighted on my resume. The interviewer also asked questions about Java collections.

Two days later, I received a call from HR confirming that I had cleared the first technical round. The HR representative was very friendly and took the opportunity to confirm a few details regarding the role and the package being offered before proceeding to the next round.

I was then invited to the second technical interview, which was conducted by a Lead Engineer with nearly 10 years of experience in Software Engineering. Since I had completed an internship and had Java-Spring Boot listed as part of my tech stack on my resume, I was asked to write demo APIs in Spring Boot and follow-up questions were posed on various topics including:

- HTTP status codes and their meanings

- The difference between Forbidden vs. Unauthorized status codes

- Indexing in databases

- User authentication and authorization flows, including JWT token flow

- SQL vs. NoSQL in depth

- PostgreSQL vs. MongoDB

- ACID vs. CAP Theorem

- Sharding and its necessity

- Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection

- Getter and Setter Injection

- The Singleton design pattern

The interview was scheduled for 35 minutes but ended up lasting an hour. We also discussed my internship experience, and I asked several questions to better understand Finzly.

The next day, the HR round was scheduled. It was conducted by the Head of HR, who asked about my background, college experience, internship work, and a few questions related to relocation and company policies.

A week later, I received an email notifying me of my selection, along with a Letter of Intent.

Pro Tips: Focus on OOP, projects, problem-solving, and Java.

experiences.title: Flipkart  Interview Experience for Application Engineer (Off-Campus)
experiences.full_content:
Recently, I had the opportunity to interview for the position of Application Engineer at Flipkart through their off-campus drive. The interview process consisted of four rounds, each designed to assess different skills and attributes required for the role. Here’s a breakdown of my experience:

Round 1: Online Assessment (1 Hour on Unstop)

The first round was an online assessment that lasted for one hour. It was divided into two sections:

MCQs (10 minutes): These questions were focused on fundamental concepts, including computer science topics like Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA), databases, and operating systems.

Coding Problems (50 minutes): The coding section involved easy to medium-level problems similar to those on LeetCode, mainly focusing on arrays and strings. The questions were DSA-based, and required knowledge of concepts like sorting, searching, and array manipulations. I found the problems approachable, but solving them within the given time required a good balance of accuracy and speed.

Round 2: Problem Solving and Data Structures (PSDS) Round

This was a one-on-one technical interview round with a Flipkart engineer. I was asked two coding questions:

2D Matrix Problem: I initially provided a brute-force approach to solve the problem, but after some discussion, I optimized it using Dynamic Programming (DP) to improve both time and space complexity.

Array Problem: This was a tricky question that required careful analysis. I initially used a brute-force solution, but then discussed an optimized approach using the Greedy algorithm for better efficiency.

I was able to solve the first problem completely, while the second one led to a fruitful discussion about optimization strategies.

Round 3: Managerial Round (30 Minutes)

After clearing the technical round, I was invited to the managerial round, which was more about testing my core knowledge and problem-solving abilities. The interviewer asked:

Core DSA Questions: For example, an array-based problem on how to calculate frequency counts, and a question on linked lists where I had to explain the approach to solving it.

Internship Experience: The interviewer asked about the projects I had worked on during my internship, the technologies I used, and how I applied them to solve real-world problems.

Scenario-Based Questions: As Flipkart is an e-commerce platform, I was asked how I would improve the application’s performance and scalability. This involved discussing which technologies could be used and how to optimize for a large-scale application.

Round 4: HR Round (10-15 Minutes)

The final round was a short HR interview. It mainly revolved around introducing myself, discussing my career aspirations, and checking whether I was aware of the specific requirements of the Application Engineer role. The conversation was light but important in assessing my fit within the company culture.

Final Outcome:

Although I went through all the rounds, I was not selected for the role. However, the experience was immensely valuable. I gained insight into how to approach problem-solving with optimization in mind, improved my communication skills in technical discussions, and learned how to handle scenario-based questions that require out-of-the-box thinking.

experiences.full_content:
Online Assessment (OA):

The Fractal OA consisted of three sections:

1. Aptitude

2. Data Interpretation

3. Communication

The difficulty level of each subsequent question increased if the previous answers were correct. As a result, the full marks varied for each candidate, and the final result was based on the percentage scored, not the absolute marks .About 20 students were shortlisted for the interviews.

Interview 1: Technical (20 minutes)

The interviewer started by asking me to introduce myself. Then, I was given some coding tasks to write in Python, which included:

Printing the Fibonacci sequence.

Checking whether a number is prime.

Next, I was asked a puzzle involving three switches and three bulbs.

The interview then moved to DBMS concepts, where I was asked about:

Normalization, its types, pros and cons ,etc.

RDBMS

Some SQL questions based on concepts like joins.

Finally, I was asked a few behavioral questions:

My strengths and weaknesses.

The debate between smart work vs. hard work: which one I prefer and what a company should seek in an employee.

At the end, the interviewer asked if I had any questions, and I asked a few.

Interview 2: HR (15 minutes)

The interviewer began by introducing herself, and then I introduced myself. She asked me:

What I knew about the company and its work.

Why I wanted to join the company.

She also asked me to explain a project she pointed out from my resume, along with a few other HR questions. These included:

Whether I was willing to relocate ?

Will I go for higher studies  ?

Where do I see myself in 5 years ?

At the end, she asked if I had any questions, and I asked a few again.

Final Verdict:

I was selected. About 5 were selected .

My Suggestions:

Be honest on your resume .

experiences.title: Frontend Developer interview experience at JTG
experiences.full_content:
Here’s a detailed breakdown of my interview experience, covering all nine rounds, leading to my selection as a Frontend Developer Intern with a Pre-Placement Offer (PPO) of 12 LPA.

1st Round: Online Assessment

The first elimination round tested concepts in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Questions ranged from basic to advanced, with a strong emphasis on JavaScript topics like promises and async operations. With negative marking, accuracy was crucial for clearing this round.

2nd Round: DSA Online Test

The second elimination round focused on Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA). It included two compulsory problems:

String manipulation.
Array manipulation.
Both problems required solutions with O(1) space complexity, adding an extra layer of challenge.

3rd Round: Personality Test

This non-elimination round assessed grammar and communication skills through:

Fill-in-the-blank questions testing subject-verb agreement.
Sentence repetition tasks to evaluate language fluency.
Audio-based tasks, requiring us to repeat sentences after listening.

4th Round: Home Assignment

In this elimination round, candidates were tasked with cloning a webpage using only HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The goal was to deliver a pixel-perfect design without using frameworks or libraries like Bootstrap.

Candidates who cleared this round advanced to the Gurgaon office for further assessments.

5th Round: DSA Round

This elimination round involved solving DSA problems focusing on string and array manipulation.

6th Round: Live Coding Assignment

After the DSA round, candidates completed a live coding task to build a to-do application using only HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

The app required local storage for data persistence.
The technical interview in this round was based on the live coding task, focusing on implementation details and optimization.

7th and 8th Rounds: Technical Interviews

These two back-to-back technical interviews were elimination rounds. They covered:

Advanced HTML, CSS, and JavaScript concepts.
Additional DSA problems to test problem-solving and algorithmic thinking.

9th Round: HR Interview

The final round focused on assessing personality traits, career aspirations, and alignment with the company’s values.

Verdict: Selected

From my college, only two students were selected for the role. We joined the company in September 2024 as Frontend Developer Interns, receiving a Pre-Placement Offer (PPO) of 12 LPA.

experiences.title: Futures First Interview Experience with  for  Market Analyst Trainee Role
extracted_questions: Why Futures First?
How would you handle stress and risk in a market analyst role?
experiences.full_content:
In September 2024, Futures First visited VIT to recruit for the Trainee – Market Analyst role. Here's a detailed breakdown of the entire process, along with my personal experience, tips, and insights.

The recruitment process took place in a single day and consisted of the following stages:

Online Assessment (Round 1)
Group Discussion (Round 2)
Technical and Behavioral Interviews (Round 3 & 4)
The process was intense, but if you're quick with numbers, have a good grasp of financial markets, and can manage pressure, you'll have a good chance of succeeding.

Round 1: Online Assessment

Number of candidates: 4000+
Shortlisted for the next round: 57–60
This round was all about logical reasoning, quantitative aptitude, and quick math problems. The key challenge here was the time constraint. We had to solve around 40 quick math questions in 10 minutes. The questions ranged from basic arithmetic to logical puzzles.

Key Tips for Round 1:

Be prepared with a pen and paper for fast calculations.

Focus on speed and accuracy.

Practice mental math and common quantitative aptitude problems before the test.

My Experience: The online assessment was the trickiest part due to the time pressure. The most important thing here was to stay calm and avoid getting stuck on any question. I aimed to answer as many as possible accurately in the limited time.

Round 2: Group Discussion

Shortlisted after Round 1: Around 57 candidates
Group Size: 5–6 candidates per panel
Format: A mix of logic-based math questions, plus 1/minus 1 scoring system.
In this round, the panelists asked a set of 16 quick math and logic-based questions to each group. The format was interesting because the questions were split into four sets, each increasing in difficulty:

Set 1: +1 for correct, -1 for wrong

Set 2: +2/-2

Set 3: +3/-3

Set 4: +4/-4

This format not only tested our mathematical ability but also our decision-making skills under pressure.

Key Tips for Round 2:

Stay calm and confident, even if you miss a question.

Be quick but accurate—negative marking can hurt your chances.

Engage in the discussion and think logically.

My Experience: This round was both challenging and competitive. I focused on answering only the questions I was confident about to avoid losing points. It’s crucial to know when to answer and when to pass.

Round 3: Technical Interview

Interviewer: Vice President (for me), Senior Associates for some candidates

The first interview was more technical and finance-oriented. The questions revolved around:

Stock market basics: What are stocks, IPOs, bids, offers, etc.

Financial concepts: Futures, options, derivatives, commodity markets.

Quick math: Solving short math problems quickly.

They also asked some behavioral questions, such as:

"Why do you want to join Futures First?"

"Considering the high attrition rate, what motivates you?"

Given my computer science background, I was asked why I wanted to transition into finance. This is a common question if you're from a non-finance field, so be ready with a strong answer.

Key Tips for Round 3:

Brush up on stock market fundamentals (e.g., IPOs, futures, derivatives).
Prepare for quick math problems similar to the online test.
Have a convincing answer for why you want to join the company.
My Experience: The first interview was a mix of technical and behavioral questions. I was thoroughly prepared for the finance-related topics, and I practiced my quick math, which helped a lot. It’s important to show that you have a genuine interest in finance and trading.

Round 4: Final HR/Behavioral Interview

Interviewer: Senior employee from Futures First

The final round was more of a fitment round to assess if you’re capable of handling the pressure and fast-paced environment of the company. The questions focused on:

Why Futures First?
How would you handle stress and risk in a market analyst role?
Situational questions: E.g., how you would handle a difficult situation or make a quick decision under pressure.
This interview was shorter than the previous one but equally important, as they evaluated my ability to adapt to the high-stress environment of trading.

Key Tips for Round 4:

Be honest and confident.

Show that you can handle stress and risks.

Demonstrate a willingness to learn and grow in the role.

My Experience: The final interview was more about my personality and soft skills. They wanted to make sure I could handle the high-pressure environment that Futures First is known for. I stayed calm and answered confidently, emphasizing my interest in finance and trading.

Conclusion

The entire process was demanding but rewarding. Confidence, quick thinking, and a good understanding of financial markets are key to clearing the interview. The environment at Futures First is fast-paced and challenging, so they look for candidates who can thrive under pressure.

For anyone preparing for this role:

Focus on mental math and logic.
Understand basic financial concepts.
Be prepared for behavioral questions that test your decision-making and stress management.
Good luck to everyone aiming for this exciting and challenging role!

experiences.title: GAIL Interview Experience | GET

experiences.title: Gameskraft Interview Experiance
experiences.full_content:
The process began with a 1.5-hour Online Assessment (OA) that included one medium and two hard questions. I successfully solved all of them, which advanced me to the interview rounds.

Round 1: Technical Interview

Q1: Rotten Oranges
I was tasked with solving a problem involving a grid of oranges, where some were rotten. The objective was to determine how long it would take for all the oranges to become rotten.
Q2: House Robber
I was asked to write the recursive solution first, followed by the tabulation method, and finally optimize it to O(1) space complexity.
Q3: 0-1-2 Sort
Since there was extra time, the interviewer gave me a third problem. I was asked to implement the most optimal approach using pointers. The interviewer was satisfied with my solution.

Round 2: Technical Interview

Q1: Koko Eating Bananas
I explained the O(n log n) binary search solution, which the interviewer found satisfactory.
Q2: Low-Level Design (Library Management System)
I was asked to design a Library Management System and provide the code for it. The interviewer seemed content with my approach and implementation.
Note: This round varied for other candidates. Some were asked about OOP, DBMS, OS, or their projects and internships.

Round 3: Technical Interview

This round was held late at night, from 9:30 PM to 10:30 PM. The interviewer, who held a director-level position, had his child on his lap throughout the interview, and it was clear he wasn’t fully engaged in the process. He asked random implementation-based questions, seemingly just to pass the time. Regardless, I completed the tasks, and he appeared satisfied with my code.

Issues with the Process

To my disappointment, the HR rounds had already taken place, and candidates had been selected before my interview was conducted. It seemed as though they were rushing through the process due to the late hour. Moreover, my interviews were delayed multiple times, which I found unprofessional and frustrating.

experiences.title: GE Healthcare Interview Experience | SDE Internship | On Campus
experiences.full_content:
In this post, I’ll share my interview experience with GE Healthcare during their visit to our campus, SVNIT Surat, in August 2024, for hiring 2-month interns under the Tech Intern role in the EEDP Program.

Eligibility Criteria

CGPA Requirement: Students with a CGPA greater than 7 were eligible.
Eligible Branches: CSE, ECE, and Electrical.

Online Assessment

The first round was an Online Assessment that tested coding and aptitude skills. The test lasted for 2 hours and included questions on:

Coding
English
Logical Reasoning
Aptitude

Coding Questions

The coding questions were unique for each student. Here’s what I faced:

248 Number Problem:

A number is considered valid if digits 2, 4, and 8 occur in it with equal nonzero frequencies. For example:
Valid: 248, 284824, 2148
Invalid: 3456 (unequal frequencies), 356 (zero frequencies)

The task was to count valid numbers in the range [1, n], where 1 ≤ n ≤ 10¹⁰.

Pencils Problem:

Given an array where each number represents the length of a pencil, determine the minimum height remaining after performing the operation:
1 operation - Cut a pencil to any length.
The 248 Number question was partially solved, while the Pencils question was fully solved.

Some of my peers encountered different problems, such as:

Zig-Zag Traversal of a Binary Tree
Euler Cycle in a Graph

Technical Interview (30 Minutes)

The Technical Interview began with a brief introduction. The interviewer was friendly and created a comfortable environment. Here’s what followed:

Questions on Programming

The interviewer asked about my proficiency in programming languages. Since I mentioned C++, most questions revolved around Object-Oriented Programming (OOPS):

Copy Constructor:

Explanation and a real-life example.

Virtual Function & Function Overriding:

Definition and usage in development.

Project Discussion

The interviewer asked about my web development projects and work on the MERN stack. Additionally, they inquired about my participation in the Amazon ML Summer School and posed a simple question:

"Gemini/ChatGPT uses which type of Machine Learning?"

Verdict: Cleared for the HR Round.

HR Round

The HR Round focused on general and behavioral questions:

Competitors of GE Healthcare
Willingness to relocate
Familiarity with GE Healthcare products
Verdict: Rejected.

Despite clearing the technical round, I wasn’t selected in the HR round. However, the experience was enriching and offered valuable insights.

Tips for Future Aspirants

Focus on DSA and Core Subjects:

Prepare topics like OOPS and Operating Systems thoroughly.

Stay Calm and Confident:

Maintaining composure during interviews can make a big difference.

Configuration and Management: Demonstrate your ability to configure and manage FortiClient and FortiAnalyzer in diverse network environments.
