experiences.title: How to Get an Internship as a Data Quality Analyst
experiences.full_content:
Securing an internship as a Data Quality Analyst is a crucial step towards a data management and analysis career. This role involves ensuring data accuracy, consistency, and reliability, which is essential for informed decision-making within organizations. Aspiring Data Quality Analysts must develop technical skills in SQL, Python, and data tools, build a compelling resume and portfolio, and network with industry professionals.

Data Quality Analyst This guide provides a comprehensive roadmap to How to Get an Internship as a Data Quality Analyst, from skill development to interview preparation, to help you successfully land an internship and begin your journey in the field of data quality analysis.

Table of Content

Understanding the Role of a Data Quality Analyst
Educational Background and Relevant Courses
Develop Relevant Skills
Create a Strong Resume
Build a Portfolio
Network with Professionals
Apply to Internships
Prepare for Interviews

Understanding the Role of a Data Quality Analyst

A Data Quality Analyst is responsible for ensuring that an organization's data assets are accurate, consistent, and reliable. They play a pivotal role in identifying and rectifying data quality issues, establishing data quality standards, and implementing processes to maintain high data integrity. By doing so, they help organizations maximize the value of their data and support data-driven decision-making.

Key Responsibilities of Data Quality Analyst

Data Quality Analysts have a arrange of responsibilities, including:

Conducting data quality assessments and audits.
Identifying data anomalies and inconsistencies.
Developing and implementing data quality standards and processes.
Collaborating with data stewards and IT teams to resolve data quality issues.
Monitoring data quality metrics and reporting findings.
Providing recommendations for data quality improvements.

Educational Background and Relevant Courses

Degree Programs

To become a Data Quality Analyst, a background in the following degree programs can be beneficial:

Computer Science
Information Technology
Data Science
Business Analytics

Essential Courses and Certifications

Key courses and certifications include:

SQL for Data Management
Data Governance
Data Quality Management
Certification in Data Management (e.g., CDMP from DAMA International)

Online Learning Resources

Online platforms like GeeksforGeeks, Coursera, edX, and Udacity offer relevant courses and certifications that can enhance your knowledge and skills in data quality management.

Develop Relevant Skills

To excel as a Data Quality Analyst, you'll need to cultivate a variety of skills:

Technical Skills:

SQL: Learn how to write and optimize SQL queries to retrieve and manipulate data from databases.
Python/R: Gain proficiency in programming languages commonly used for data analysis and automation of data quality tasks.
Data Tools: Familiarize yourself with data quality tools like Talend, Informatica, or Microsoft Data Quality Services.

Data Management:

Data Warehousing: Understand the principles of data warehousing and how data is structured and stored.
ETL Processes: Learn about ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) processes, which are essential for data integration and quality management.
Data Governance: Study data governance practices, including data standards, policies, and compliance requirements.

Analytical Skills:

Data Analysis: Develop strong analytical skills to identify data inconsistencies, errors, and patterns.
Problem-Solving: Enhance your ability to troubleshoot data issues and implement solutions.

Attention to Detail:

Precision: Cultivate a meticulous approach to working with data to ensure its accuracy and quality.

Communication Skills:

Reporting: Learn how to effectively communicate data quality findings and recommendations to stakeholders.
Collaboration: Develop interpersonal skills to work collaboratively with data engineers, analysts, and other team members.

Create a Strong Resume

Your resume is your first impression to potential employers. Ensure it effectively highlights your relevant skills, education, and experience:

Education:

Degree: List your degree, major, and institution. Highlight any coursework related to data analysis, database management, or statistics.
Certifications: Mention relevant certifications, such as Microsoft Certified: Data Analyst Associate or Certified Data Management Professional (CDMP).

Experience:

Internships: Detail any previous internships or part-time jobs related to data quality, analysis, or IT.
Projects: Include academic or personal projects that demonstrate your ability to work with data. Describe your role and the impact of your work.

Skills:

Technical Skills: List your proficiency in SQL, Python, R, and any data quality tools.
Soft Skills: Highlight your analytical thinking, problem-solving abilities, and communication skills.

Build a Portfolio

A strong portfolio can significantly enhance your application by showcasing your practical experience and expertise:

Projects:

Academic Projects: Include projects from your coursework that involved data analysis or quality assurance.
Personal Projects: Highlight personal initiatives where you identified and resolved data quality issues.

Case Studies:

Detailed Descriptions: Provide in-depth case studies of projects where you improved data quality. Describe the problem, your approach, and the outcomes.

GitHub Profile:

Repositories: Share your GitHub profile with repositories of your work. Ensure your code is well-documented and demonstrates your skills.

Network with Professionals

Networking can open doors to internship opportunities and provide valuable insights into the industry:

Joining Professional Associations

Joining associations like DAMA International can provide networking opportunities, access to industry resources, and professional development.

Attending Industry Conferences and Meetups

Industry conferences and meetups are great venues to learn about the latest trends, meet industry professionals, and expand your professional network.

Leveraging LinkedIn and Other Professional Networks

Use LinkedIn and other professional networks to connect with industry professionals, join relevant groups, and stay updated on industry news.

Apply to Internships

When you're ready to apply, follow these steps to increase your chances of success:

Job Boards:

Listings: Use job boards like Indeed, Glassdoor, and LinkedIn to find internship opportunities.

Company Websites:

Career Pages: Regularly check the career pages of companies you're interested in for internship listings.

University Career Services:

Resources: Utilize your university’s career services for internship listings, resume reviews, and application assistance.

Tailor Your Applications:

Customization: Customize your resume and cover letter for each application, highlighting how your skills and experience align with the job description.
Keywords: Incorporate relevant keywords from the job listing to pass through Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS).

Prepare for Interviews

Research the Company:

Background: Understand the company's mission, values, and products or services.
Role Understanding: Familiarize yourself with the role of data quality within the organization.

Practice Common Questions:

Technical Questions: Prepare for questions related to data analysis, SQL, ETL processes, and data quality tools.
Behavioral Questions: Practice answers to behavioral questions that assess your problem-solving skills, attention to detail, and ability to work in a team.

Showcase Your Portfolio:

Projects: Be ready to discuss your portfolio projects in detail, explaining your role, the challenges you faced, and the outcomes.
Impact: Highlight how your work improved data quality and benefited the project or organization.

Conclusion

Securing an internship as a Data Quality Analyst requires a blend of technical skills, meticulous resume crafting, and strategic networking. Develop expertise in SQL, Python, data management, and analysis. Build a strong resume and a portfolio showcasing relevant projects. Network through LinkedIn, industry events, and informational interviews. Apply to internships with tailored applications and prepare thoroughly for interviews by researching companies and practicing both technical and behavioral questions. By following these steps, you can effectively position yourself to land an internship and kickstart your career in data quality analysis.

experiences.title: How to Get an Internship as an Operations Research Analyst
experiences.full_content:
Operations research analysts play a crucial role in optimizing decision-making processes within organizations. Internships in this field provide invaluable opportunities for students and recent graduates to gain practical experience and apply theoretical knowledge to real-world scenarios. Securing an internship as an Operations Research (OR) Analyst can be a pivotal step in your career journey. Internships provide invaluable hands-on experience, industry connections, and a deeper understanding of how theoretical knowledge is applied in real-world settings.

How to Get an Internship as an Operations Research AnalystThis article explores the significance of Operations Research Analyst Internships, outlines key responsibilities and skills required, discusses how to prepare effectively, and offers tips for securing and excelling in these internships.

Table of Content

Understanding Operations Research Analyst Roles
Develop Relevant Skills
Create a Strong Resume
Build a Portfolio
Network with Professionals
Apply to Internships
Prepare for Interviews

Understanding Operations Research Analyst Roles

Operations research analysts apply mathematical and analytical methods to help organizations solve complex problems and make informed decisions. They work across various industries, applying their skills in areas such as logistics, supply chain management, finance, healthcare, and more.

Key Responsibilities and Skills Required

Operations research analyst interns typically assist in:

Data Analysis: Collecting, cleaning, and analyzing data using statistical methods and optimization techniques.
Model Development: Building mathematical models to simulate scenarios and predict outcomes.
Decision Support: Providing actionable recommendations based on data-driven insights.

Develop Relevant Skills

To stand out as a candidate, you must develop a robust skill set that aligns with the demands of the operations research field. Focus on the following areas:

Mathematics and Statistics: Master advanced topics in calculus, linear algebra, probability, and statistical methods, as these are crucial for modelling and solving optimization problems.
Programming Languages: Proficiency in programming languages such as Python, R, and SQL is essential. Python and R are particularly useful for statistical analysis and data visualization, while SQL is important for managing and querying large datasets.
Optimization Techniques: Gain a solid understanding of optimization methods, including linear programming, integer programming, nonlinear programming, and dynamic programming. Familiarity with software like Gurobi, CPLEX, or MATLAB is also beneficial.
Simulation: Learn simulation techniques and tools such as Monte Carlo simulations, discrete-event simulations, and agent-based models. Software like Simul8 or Arena can be helpful.
Data Analysis: Develop strong data analysis skills, including data cleaning, data visualization, and exploratory data analysis. Tools like Excel, Tableau, and specialized OR software should be in your toolkit.

Create a Strong Resume

Your resume is a critical marketing tool that showcases your qualifications. Ensure it highlights the following:

Education: List your degree(s), relevant coursework, and any honors or awards. Highlight classes that are particularly pertinent to operations research.
Skills: Clearly list technical skills, including programming languages, software tools, and analytical techniques.
Projects: Detail any academic or personal projects that demonstrate your ability to apply OR techniques to solve real-world problems. Include specifics about your role, the methodologies you used, and the outcomes achieved.
Experience: If you have any related work experience, such as internships, part-time jobs, or volunteer work, describe your responsibilities and achievements in detail.

Build a Portfolio

A portfolio can provide concrete evidence of your skills and experience. Include:

Project Descriptions: Summarize projects you've worked on, detailing your role, the methodologies you applied, and the results. Highlight any projects that involved significant data analysis, optimization, or simulation.
Code Samples: Provide examples of your programming work, especially those that demonstrate your ability to implement OR techniques. Include well-documented code that shows your problem-solving approach.
Reports and Visualizations: Include any analytical reports or data visualizations you’ve created. These can illustrate your ability to communicate complex information effectively.

Network with Professionals

Networking is crucial for uncovering internship opportunities and gaining industry insights.

Here’s how to build a strong professional network:

Attend Industry Events: Participate in conferences, workshops, and seminars related to operations research. Events hosted by organizations like INFORMS are particularly valuable.
Join Professional Organizations: Become a member of professional organizations such as INFORMS, which offer networking opportunities, resources, and events.
Use Social Media: Connect with professionals on LinkedIn, join relevant groups, and participate in discussions. Follow companies and thought leaders in the OR field.
Informational Interviews: Reach out to OR professionals for informational interviews. These conversations can provide insights into the field, advice on career paths, and potential job leads.

Apply to Internships

When you’re ready to apply, use multiple channels to maximize your opportunities:

Job Boards: Use job boards like Indeed, Glassdoor, and specialized sites for OR and analytics positions. Websites like OR Jobs and INFORMS Career Center are also useful.
Company Websites: Check the careers pages of companies known for their OR departments or analytics teams. Many companies post internships directly on their websites.
University Career Centers: Leverage your school’s career services, which often have listings and connections with employers seeking interns. Attend career fairs and workshops offered by your university.
Professional Networks: Utilize your network to discover hidden opportunities. Let your contacts know you’re looking for an internship and ask for referrals.

Prepare for Interviews

Once you secure an interview, thorough preparation is key to success:

Review Basic Concepts: Refresh your knowledge of fundamental OR techniques and concepts. Be prepared to discuss your understanding of optimization, simulation, and data analysis.
Practice Problem-Solving: Be ready to solve technical problems or case studies that demonstrate your analytical thinking. Practice with sample problems and case studies commonly used in OR.
Mock Interviews:Conduct mock interviews with friends, mentors, or career services. Focus on both technical and behavioral questions to improve your confidence and performance.
Questions to Ask:Prepare thoughtful questions about the company, the team, and the projects you might be working on. This shows your genuine interest and helps you assess if the internship is the right fit for you.

Networking and Professional Development

Utilizing LinkedIn and Other Professional Networks: Optimize your LinkedIn profile to highlight your skills and career interests. Join professional groups related to operations research and engage with industry professionals to expand your network.
Attending Industry Events and Conferences: Attend virtual or in-person events such as industry conferences, webinars, and workshops to stay updated on trends, connect with professionals, and explore internship opportunities.

Tips for Succeeding in Your Internship

Setting Goals and Expectations: Define specific learning goals for your internship, such as mastering new software tools or gaining exposure to different industries. Communicate these goals with your supervisor to align expectations.
Building Relationships and Seeking Mentorship: Network with colleagues and supervisors to build relationships. Seek mentorship from experienced operations research analysts to gain insights, receive guidance, and enhance your professional development.

Conclusion

Landing an internship as an Operations Research Analyst involves a strategic combination of skill development, networking, and thorough preparation. By following these steps, you can enhance your chances of securing a valuable internship that will pave the way for a successful career in operations research. Remember to stay proactive, persistent, and open to learning opportunities along the way.

experiences.title: Interview Experience of Capgemini
experiences.full_content:
Company Name: Capgemini

Job Role: Analyst

Years of Experience Required: No Experience Required

Drive: On Campus Drive

Preparation Topics:

Data Structures: Arrays, Strings, Linked Lists

DBMS: DML, DDL, Joins

Duration: The interview consists of a 30-minute session that includes both HR and technical aspects.

Source of Preparation:

Check GFG website for DSA preparation.

Review the Ultimate Resume Building Guide for coding interviews.

Explore the DBMS Course of GFG .

Round 1: Technical + Written English + Gamified

I recently participated in an On Campus drive at Capgemini, and while I was ultimately selected for a competitive package, the journey was anything but easy. In the first round, candidates face multiple sections within a single test, and progression depends on qualifying each section. The entire test lasts about 2 hours, so managing time effectively is crucial.

The technical section includes 25 MCQs focused on Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) and programming, followed by 15 questions that cover essential topics from cloud computing, operating systems (OS), and networking. Given the breadth of these topics, it’s vital to brush up on your fundamentals to stand a chance of qualifying.

Should you pass this technical section, you’ll then encounter the Written English test. In this part, you'll be required to write a 200-220 word paragraph on general topics like pollution or the effects of heatwaves on the public—this tests not only your writing skills but also your ability to articulate thoughts clearly under time constraints.

Once you clear the English test, the next hurdle is the Gamified round, which features various logical and memory games. Familiarizing yourself with similar exercises through YouTube resources can be beneficial, but the unpredictability of this section can throw many candidates off their game. After completing all the rounds, you’ll need to wait for the results. If you performed well, you can expect an invitation for the Coding round within 2-3 working days.

Round 2: Online Coding Test

This round presents a set of coding challenges designed to test your algorithmic thinking and coding skills under pressure.

Problem List:

Problem Statement: Given a linked list, return the head of the reversed Linked List.

Input Format: 1->2->3->4->5

Result: 5->4->3->2->1

Explanation: You’re provided with the head of a linked list and must return the list where the elements are reversed in order.

Problem Statement: Given a string, print the count of every character.

Input Format: Hello

Result:

H : 1

E : 1

L : 2

O : 1

These problems require not only a solid understanding of data structures but also the ability to implement efficient algorithms quickly.

Round 3: Online Technical HR Interview

In this round, the interview commenced with my introduction. The interviewer delved deeply into my projects, probing the technicalities of each. I showcased three projects, utilizing different technologies: one in Java, another in Web Development, and the third employing the Selenium framework in Python. The discussion was thorough, demanding a clear articulation of my contributions and challenges faced during each project.

Following this, I was tasked with writing two SQL queries involving simple joins. The interviewer’s scrutiny intensified as I was asked to open a notepad and write code to reverse a string. The technical questions further escalated with deep inquiries into Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) concepts, requiring me to demonstrate a nuanced understanding of the principles involved.

Additionally, I faced several challenging questions related to cloud computing, especially concerning AWS. The interviewer probed my knowledge of cloud architecture and services, making it evident that a solid grasp of these topics was essential for success.

The interview concluded with basic HR questions, leading to discussions about my goals, expectations, and flexibility. While these questions may seem straightforward, they require self-awareness and clarity about one's career aspirations.

Message to Aspiring Students:

You can navigate these challenging rounds successfully by focusing on solidifying your fundamentals. It's crucial to have a clear understanding of everything you include in your resume—only write about what you genuinely know. Avoid fabricating information or exaggerating skills to impress; honesty and confidence in your knowledge will significantly enhance your chances of success.

experiences.title: My Journey to Becoming a GFG Campus Mantri
experiences.full_content:
I still vividly remember the day I applied for the GFG Campus Mantri program. It was sometime in April, and little did I know that the journey would involve a 3-4 month wait before I received the much-anticipated confirmation that I had been shortlisted. The news came as a complete surprise—I was both thrilled and nervous about the upcoming interview.

Pre-Interview Nerves

As the interview day approached, I was overwhelmed with a mix of emotions. Doubts clouded my mind: Would I do well? Was I prepared enough? Sharing my worries with one of my closest friends turned out to be the best decision. They boosted my confidence and helped calm my nerves, reminding me to believe in myself.

The Interview Day

On the day of the interview, I was in college and had to request permission from my faculty to leave class early for the telephonic interview. As I waited for the call, my heart raced, and my nervousness grew. When the call finally came, I took a deep breath and tried to stay composed.

The interview began with a request to introduce myself, followed by the key question:
"Why do you want to be a Campus Mantri?"

Although I did my best to answer, I stumbled a few times and felt unsure about my performance. Despite my nervousness, I managed to complete the interview. However, I couldn’t shake the feeling that I hadn’t done well enough to be selected.

The Surprise Selection

To my astonishment, a few days later, I received a welcome letter from GFG, informing me that I had been selected as a Campus Mantri! The emotions that followed were indescribable—shock, happiness, and relief all at once. It was a moment of pure joy and gratitude, knowing I was now a part of the prestigious GFG community.

Lessons Learned

Looking back, this experience taught me invaluable lessons:

Facing fears: Stepping out of my comfort zone made me more resilient.
Building confidence: Believing in myself, even in moments of doubt, proved essential.
Persevering through setbacks: Mistakes are a part of growth, and persistence pays off.

Excited for the Journey Ahead

Becoming a GFG Campus Mantri has been a fulfilling milestone. I’m eager to make the most of this opportunity and contribute meaningfully to the GFG community. This journey has not only boosted my confidence but also reaffirmed the value of hard work and perseverance.

I had the opportunity to participate in the National Payments Corporation of India's (NPCI) off-campus recruitment process for the Graduate Engineer Trainee (GET) role. The process consisted of three elimination rounds. Here are the details:

Online Assessment 1 (Aptitude & Technical MCQ's (Python, numPY)
Online Assessment 2 (Coding Round)

Applied on: 21st November, 2023

Round 1: Online Assessment 1  (60 min) ( 23rd Dec 2023)

The first round of the recruitment process was an online assessment consisting of two sections: Aptitude and Technical MCQs.

The Aptitude section was further divided into two sub-sections:

- Quantitative Aptitude

- Reasoning Ability

Each sub-section contained 20 questions, and a total of 40 minutes was provided to solve both. During this time, candidates were allowed to navigate between the sub-sections. After completing the Aptitude section, the Technical MCQ section began. This section consisted of 20 questions to be solved within 20 minutes. The questions primarily focused on Python libraries, such as NumPy and scikit-learn, as well as outputs of code snippets and SQL.

Tip: Use your time wisely to ensure you can answer all questions effectively.

Assesment Platform: cocubes

Round 2: Online Assessment 2 (45 min ) ( 2nd Mar 2024)

The second round was a coding assessment, featuring two questions to be solved within 45 minutes.

The first question was straightforward and required implementing basic if-else conditions.
The second question was a direct LeetCode medium-level problem.
The coding round was not particularly difficult and could be easily cleared with a basic understanding of coding concepts.

Round 3: Technical Interview ( 45 min) ( 4th Apr 2024)

The third round was a Technical + HR Interview with a panel comprising two technical interviewers and one HR representative. HR interviewer began by asking me to introduce myself. Following this, the technical interviewers took over and primarily focused on my project. You should have a clear understanding of the project architecture, workflow, and the underlying code. They also asked me to write small code snippets related to my project.Additionally, they tested my knowledge on concepts such as Authentication, Authorization, and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). Strong explanation skills are crucial to succeeding in this round.

experiences.full_content:
ZS Interview Experience: Fresher

I applied through a referral for the DAA role at ZS in May 2024. After about 45 days, I received the test link for Round 1. The entire process is divided into four rounds.

ROUND 1 : APTITUDE ROUND :

In this round, there are a total of 6 sections:

Numerical Ability,
Verbal Ability,
Analytical Ability,
Guesstimates,
Critical Thinking,
and Attention to Detail.

Each section has a specific time duration, and the number of questions in each section varies.

Speed is key to clearing this round.

NOTE : The Guesstimate section is the most crucial. It contains two hard-level questions, and the total time for that section is 14 minutes. If you solve both of them correctly, or at least one correctly, your chances of clearing the round increase significantly.

I received an email for Round 2 a week after completing Round 1.

Round 2: CASE STUDY ROUND :

This is the easiest and least eliminative round in the process. You are given a case study, and based on that, some MCQs or theory questions, which you have to solve. All MCQs are solved using data interpretation.

For me, the time duration was 1 hour, and there were 3 MCQs and 1 theory question.

ROUND 3 : INTERVIEW ( Case Study + Technical ) ROUND :

On the same day as the Case Study round, I received a call for this round. The round lasted for 25-30 minutes. In this round, the interviewer mainly focused on discussing the case study I had solved during Round 2. Additionally, he asked some puzzles. The interview went well, and he mentioned that HR would contact me for the further process.

Four to five days later, I received a call from HR for the final interview round.

ROUND 4 : INTERVIEW ( Technical + Hr) ROUND :

The interview began with my introduction, followed by questions about the projects I mentioned in my resume and my internship. After a long discussion on those topics, she started asking puzzles. She inquired whether I had heard about the puzzles before or not.

She asked a total of three puzzles, and I answered all of them correctly. For each puzzle, she asked about my approach to solving it.

After that, she asked a few HR questions like:

Why ZS?
What do you know about ZS?
Why should we hire you?
Why did you choose the Analytics field?
We had a discussion on all the questions, and she seemed satisfied with most of my answers. The interview lastly for about 1 hour.

Verdict: Selected

A few days later, I received a call from HR with the news:

Congratulations!

I was selected for the DAA profile at ZS.

The joining was scheduled after the completion of the degree, and the compensation package offered ranged between ₹630,000 to ₹700,000 per annum. The work location was PAN India.

Hiring Process Overview

The hiring process for the Genpact role consisted of the following rounds:

Speech Test
Pre-Placement Talk
Online Test
Group Discussion
Technical Interview
Project Submission

Round 1: Speech Test

The first round was the Speech Test, which was designed to assess your listening, speaking, and writing skills. This round tested your communication abilities, including clarity, coherence, and language proficiency.

Round 2: Pre-Placement Talk

The second round was the Pre-Placement Talk, where the company provided an overview of Genpact as an organization. This session included key information about the company’s culture, the role being offered, salary distribution, and the probation period of 4 to 6 months.

Round 3: Online Test

The third round was an online assessment, where the focus was on testing your computer science fundamentals and coding skills. The difficulty of the coding questions ranged from easy to medium. In addition to coding, the test also included questions related to general problem-solving and logical reasoning.

Round 4: Group Discussion

The fourth round was a Group Discussion (GD), held offline. This round was crucial as it served as the main elimination round. The panel evaluated candidates based on their soft skills, including communication, teamwork, and how effectively they could express their opinions in a group setting. Strong interpersonal skills were a key factor for selection in this round.

Round 5: Technical Interview

In the Technical Interview round, candidates were asked about language-specific fundamentals, Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) concepts, and basic coding questions. The interview was relatively straightforward, but it was important to demonstrate a solid understanding of programming principles and problem-solving skills.

Round 6: Project Submission

The final round was the Project Submission. After the technical interview, candidates were given a deadline to create and submit a real-world full-stack working project. This project was the deciding factor for many candidates. Those who completed and submitted the project within the given timeframe were selected for the role.

Conclusion

Genpact’s hiring process is thorough, with each round designed to assess different aspects of a candidate’s abilities, from communication and soft skills to technical expertise and project execution. The process includes a mix of individual and group activities, and a strong performance in all rounds is essential to securing the position.

Good luck to anyone preparing for Genpact's placement process!

experiences.title: Genpact Interview Experience | On Campus
experiences.full_content:
Genpact visited our college for hiring during the month of August 2023, It had visited our college after 10 years so we had 0 clue of how and what process they would conduct. They were offering the role of Technical Associate with a package of 4.7lpa.

Its hiring started with a briefing about the company where some experts from the company briefed us about the company, work culture, and the overall hiring process.

Soon after the briefing, there were 3 rounds:

Online Test
Group Discussion
Technical and HR interview round

Online Test

After 2 days of the briefing, a test link was sent to us which consisted of questions from various sections like Programming language, Basic DSA questions like a linked list, tree, graph, etc., Computer networking, OS, DBMS, Gen-AI, etc.

After the test results were declared, out of 480 students only 180 students were able to qualify for the next round which was the GD round.

Group Discussion

This was held a week or so after the online test, here they had divided the students into groups and each group was allotted a different time for a smooth process. Initially, for a few groups, the topics were the same but later after I think group 4 the topics were changed and each group now had a different topic, once you entered the meeting they briefed about the session and gave a topic and 2min time to think and analyze the topic. A total of 10 students were there in my group, and we were given hardly 8 minutes to speak. I got the topic "Social media is a boon or curse?".

After the GD round was over, out of 180 students only 63 were able to clear the round.

Technical /HR Interview

My interview was held the day after the results were declared, I was a bit nervous as well as it was the first interview I was attending. However, once the interview started I felt eased with the interviewer as she was very welcoming and very calm while trying her best to make the interview in a friendly manner.

The questions I was asked were:

Introduce yourself
Give a brief about the projects you have mentioned
I was asked 3-4 questions each from each project specially from my ML projects like which model i used and why i used , how did i calculate the accuracy , What is the difference between between types of the metrics used. etc

My interview was of around 20-25min

Leetcode medium problems.

Self introduction.
Family background.

GOOD LUCK!!

experiences.title: Globallogic - Hitachi Interview Experience (On-Campus)
experiences.full_content:
The GlobalLogic Hitachi on-campus hiring process began with an online registration through my college’s portal. Once registered, the first round was scheduled for 21st August 2024. This round was an online test that lasted for 124 minutes. The test was comprehensive, covering various aspects:

30 questions on computer fundamentals: These questions tested our understanding of core subjects like Operating Systems, Networks, Data Structures, and Algorithms.

10 aptitude questions: These questions evaluated our logical reasoning, mathematical skills, and problem-solving abilities.

Email writing task: This tested our communication skills, particularly how well we could convey information in a professional format.

2 coding questions: The coding problems were of medium difficulty. The first question revolved around XOR operations, which required a good understanding of bitwise operations. The second question involved a sliding window problem, testing our ability to handle and optimize window-based data processing.

Out of the 356 students who took the test, only 40 were shortlisted for the next round. This initial filtering was rigorous, ensuring that only candidates with strong foundational knowledge and problem-solving ability moved forward.

Round 2: Technical Interview

The second round was a technical interview, held virtually on 29th August 2024. The interview lasted around 30-40 minutes and began with a warm greeting from the interviewer, setting a comfortable tone for the conversation.

The questions asked were focused on core technical concepts, including:

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): I was asked to explain the 4 pillars of OOP—encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction.

Data Structures: The interviewer inquired about trees and graphs, asking me to explain their structure and differences.

Coding tasks: I was given a few coding challenges during the interview, including:

Writing a code to reverse a linked list.

Writing a code to find the occurrence of the character 'a' in my name.

Writing a code to swap two numbers without using a third variable.

Database Management Systems (DBMS): I was asked about the basics of DBMS, along with different DBMS commands.

This round was crucial as it tested not only my knowledge but also my ability to apply concepts in real-time. Out of the 40 students interviewed, 30 managed to clear this technical round.

Round 3: Managerial Interview

The third round was a managerial interview, which was held shortly after the technical round. This interview lasted about 30 minutes and was more in-depth compared to the previous rounds. The interviewer started by discussing my project work, delving into the technical stack I used, the challenges I faced, and how I overcame them.

The questions in this round included:

Database-related queries: I was asked to differentiate between DDL (Data Definition Language), DML (Data Manipulation Language), and DCL (Data Control Language). Additionally, I was asked to write a SQL query to find the name and salary of employees born before 1991.

OOP Concepts: There were further discussions on OOP concepts, specifically the difference between abstraction and polymorphism, and how these concepts are applied in real-world scenarios.

Inheritance: The interviewer probed into inheritance, asking for examples and its applications.

This round was designed to assess my problem-solving approach, project management skills, and how well I could handle technical challenges in a managerial context. Clearing this round was a significant milestone, as it led me to the final HR interview.

Round 4: HR Interview

The final round was the HR interview, which primarily focused on my personality, communication skills, and cultural fit within the company. The questions were more general, aiming to understand my motivations, strengths, weaknesses, and how I handle various situations.

Questions like “Why do you want to join GlobalLogic?”, “Where do you see yourself in the next 5 years?”, and “Describe a challenging situation you’ve faced and how you handled it” were asked.

The HR round was more relaxed compared to the technical and managerial rounds but equally important as it determined whether I would fit well with the company’s culture.

Out of the 40 students who reached the HR round, 24 were finally selected to join GlobalLogic Hitachi. I am thrilled to share that I was one of the selected candidates. This entire process was a challenging yet rewarding experience, and I’m excited to start my journey with GlobalLogic.

experiences.full_content:
I got to know about this opportunity from one of my friend who works at Goldman Sachs. He referred me for the Analyst role. After I submitted my application, I got the call from recruiter that I will be receiving the online test link and I have to submit the test in next 4-5 days.

Round – 1 (Online Assessment):

2 medium level coding questions were given which I had to solve in 120 minutes. I solved both the questions and submitted the test. After few days I got a call from the recruiter to schedule the coder pad round.

Round – 2 (Coder pad round):

It was 1 hr long interview and one interviewer was present. First he introduced himself and asked me to introduce myself. Then he asked couple of follow up questions based on my introduction. Then he asked me join the coderpad link and shared the coding problem over there.

Problem 1: To find first non-repeating character in a string : https://leetcode.com/problems/first-unique-character-in-a-string/description/ I first told him brute force approach using 2 loops and of course interviewer was not happy with this then he asked me if I can optimize the solution. Then I explained him the solution using Hashmap and I wrote the code and all the test cases passed. Then he gave me one more problem.

Problem 2: To find the Best Average grade of the students: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/find-maximum-average-marks-in-student-pairs/ . This was also a map problem. I explained the solution using 2 maps: one to keep track of scores and other to keep track of frequency. I wrote the code and all the test cased passed. Interviewer was happy with this solution but he asked me if there is any way that I can optimize this. I explained him that instead of using two hash maps, I can only use one where Key will be student name and for value, I can use the custom pair class having score and frequency.

Interviewer was satisfied with this and he asked me if I have any questions. I asked questions regarding the tech stack they use in their team.

After few days I got a call from recruiter that there will be further 3 rounds all on the same day, two technical rounds which will be eliminatory and one HR round after that.

Round 3 (Technical):

It was one hour round and two interviewers were present. They introduced themselves first and asked me to introduce myself. Then they asked me few questions on my current role in current company. My current role is Data Analytics engineer so he asked me few questions related to that and asked me to explain the SDLC of it.

Then he asked me write some SQL queries:

1.	There is a patient table and I have mistakenly entered one duplicate record in it. I want to delete one record out of it. Write a SQL query for it.

Then he moved on to the coding question.

Coding Question: https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-repeating-substring/description/

Maximum Repeating Substring: For a sequence 's' and a word 'w', 'w' is said to be k-repeating in 's' if 'w' concatenated 'k' times is a substring of 's'. The word's maximum k repeating value is the highest value of k. If 'w' is not a substring of 's', value of 'k' is 0. Given 's' and 'w', find the maximum value of 'k'.

Contraints : s.length

experiences.title: Goldman Sachs Interview Experience| Summer Intern| Off-Campus
experiences.full_content:
Interviewing at Goldman Sachs for a summer internship was an exciting and enriching experience. The process was conducted entirely online in late November, comprising multiple stages designed to test both technical expertise and problem-solving skills. Here’s a breakdown of the journey, from the initial tests to the final interviews.

Pre-Interview Process

The initial step was a two-hour online test, which evaluated logical reasoning, situational analysis, and English language proficiency. Following this, a technical test was conducted, focusing on coursework and technical knowledge. Candidates who successfully cleared these tests were invited to the interview rounds.

Round 1: Technical and Behavioral

The first interview was conducted via Zoom. After joining a common waiting room, candidates were randomly called into individual interview sessions.

Key Details:

Introduction: The interviewer introduced himself and asked for a brief self-introduction. We also reviewed my resume, focusing on the projects I had worked on.
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): I was asked to explain OOP principles and code an example of encapsulation using a car-related scenario in C++.
Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA): The interviewer presented the coin change problem and asked for an optimized solution using dynamic programming. After sharing my approach, we discussed alternative solutions and their complexities.
After the interview, I was sent back to the common waiting room. The decision to progress to the next round was communicated via email later.

Round 2: Advanced Technical

Shortlisted candidates were invited to the second round the next day. Like before, communication and the interview were handled through Zoom.

Key Details:

DSA Focus: The round was entirely DSA-based. I was given two problems related to arrays and strings. The task was to write optimized code and explain my approach in detail.
Resume Discussion: We delved deeper into my resume, discussing my past projects and their practical applications.
After this round, candidates were moved to a post-interview waiting room. Final results, including progression to the HR round or the end of the process, were shared later.

Conclusion

The Goldman Sachs interview process was both challenging and rewarding. It tested my technical skills, problem-solving abilities, and adaptability to an online format. Regardless of the outcome, the experience was incredibly enriching and provided valuable insights into technical and professional growth.

experiences.title: Google Developer Group (GDG) Interview Experience for Campus Organizer Role

I made sure to highlight the projects that had real-world applications, showing that I wasn't just coding for practice but to make a difference.

Ethical Scenarios: Handling Tough Situations

One of the toughest questions was, "What if a lead takes money from students?" This question tested my ethical standards. I explained that integrity is crucial in any leadership role. If I found out that a lead was involved in such behavior, I would immediately investigate and take necessary action to ensure transparency and trust within the group.

Selecting Team Leads: Choosing the Right People

I was also asked about how I would select team leads. I shared that I would look for individuals who not only have technical skills but also share the values of GDG. I would prioritize those who are dedicated, have strong leadership potential, and are genuinely passionate about building a tech community.

Handling Rule-Breaking: Maintaining Discipline

Another important question was, "What if you find a lead breaking the rules?" I explained that maintaining discipline is essential for any group to function well. If a lead was found breaking rules, I would address the issue directly and ensure they understood the importance of following guidelines. Depending on the severity, I would take appropriate actions to maintain the integrity of the group.

One of the biggest concerns was how I would manage my time, balancing studies, internships, placements, and GDG responsibilities. I responded that I would prioritize my tasks, create a detailed schedule, and set realistic goals to ensure I could handle all my commitments without sacrificing my academic performance.

After the interview, I had to wait three months for the results. It felt like a long time, and during those months, I often wondered if I had done enough to secure the role. It was a time of reflection and growth as I continued to stay involved in tech activities.

Now that I’ve been selected, I’m excited to start this new chapter. I’m eager to work with other passionate individuals, organize events, and build a strong tech community on campus. This role is more than just a title; it’s an opportunity to lead, learn, and make a lasting impact. I can’t wait to see where this journey takes me.

If there's one thing I learned from this experience, it's that confidence in your abilities and values is key. No matter how challenging the questions were or how long the wait felt, I trusted in my skills and my passion for what I do. To anyone aspiring to take on a role like this, remember: if you believe in yourself and stay true to your goals, you can achieve anything. The journey may be tough, but the rewards are worth every moment. You've got what it takes—just go for it!

experiences.title: Google Developer Groups  Lead Interview Expeirence | On Campus | Selected
experiences.full_content:
GDSC Lead at Our College

Becoming the first Google Developer Groups on campus Organizer (Formerly Google Developer Student Clubs - GDSC Lead) at our college has been an incredible journey, and I’m excited to share my experience with you. As someone who was initially drawn to GDSC through events hosted by nearby colleges and the Chennai chapter, I never imagined I’d be leading the establishment of our own GDSC chapter on campus.

The Inspiration

It all started when I actively participated in GDSC events, engaging with the community, learning new skills, and attending insightful sessions. The more I learned, the more I thought, “What if we bring this to our own campus?” That’s when the idea struck me: why not establish a GDSC chapter here and offer these opportunities to our university’s students?

Getting the Green Light

Since this was the first time we were introducing GDSC at our college, I knew I needed the support of the faculty and administration. I approached our student coordinators, faculty advisors, and Head of Department with a well-prepared plan. After several discussions, they approved the idea, recognizing the potential GDSC had to enhance the technical and leadership skills of students.

With the green light, I was ready to begin the application process.

Step 1: Exploring the GDSC Application Process

I started by visiting the official GDSC Leads page: Google Developer Student Clubs Leads. For those interested, even if you miss the application window, you can sign up to receive notifications for the next cycle.

Source: Taken from GDSC advocu dashboad

Step 2: The Application Process

The application process was comprehensive. I had to provide detailed information about myself, including links to my GitHub, LinkedIn, and other platforms that showcased my technical experience. Additionally, there were several questions about my motivation for leading a GDSC, my leadership experience, and my interest in technology.

A key part of the application was a 90-second video where I needed to explain why I was the right candidate to lead the GDSC. This video allowed me to highlight my vision for the club and my commitment to the student community. I spent considerable time preparing for it, ensuring my answers were thoughtful and well-articulated.

Step 3: Application Review and Chapter Validation

After submitting my application on March 27, 2024, the GDSC team began verifying my details and validating our chapter’s eligibility. Although you can add referrals from other GDSC leads to strengthen your application, I chose not to, relying solely on my qualifications. However, I believe that a referral doesn't significantly affect your chances of being selected. If you have a strong application, you'll likely be chosen even without one.

Step 4: The Diagnostic Test

On March 29, I received the link to a 60-minute diagnostic test, which I could take any time before April 8. This test assessed my problem-solving abilities, leadership potential, and technical aptitude. I made sure to complete the test when I was fully prepared and focused, as this would play a crucial role in the next steps.

Step 5: The Interview

Following the diagnostic test, I received an email on April 24 informing me that I had qualified for the interview. The interview was scheduled for April 29, 2024.

I joined the meeting five minutes early and was greeted by a friendly interviewer. The questions focused on both technical and managerial aspects. Many were scenario-based, testing my leadership qualities, communication skills, and ability to handle team coordination in various situations. Some questions included: What challenges have you faced as a leader? How did you overcome them? Why do you want to become a GDSC lead?

I found myself speaking for most of the interview, which felt like an opportunity to express my genuine passion for leadership and community-building.

Step 6: The Results

After a long wait, I finally received the email on August 29, 2024, informing me that I had been selected as the GDSC Lead for our campus for the 2024-25 academic year! This was a moment of immense pride and excitement.

Source: Email from GDG on campus

Final Thoughts

My journey to becoming a GDSC Lead has been filled with learning and growth. The selection process challenged me to reflect on my leadership capabilities and technical expertise. I’m looking forward to using this platform to empower other students and help our campus community thrive.

As Roy T. Bennett said, “Great leaders create more leaders, not followers.” This is the ethos I plan to bring to our GDSC chapter, and I can’t wait to see the impact we’ll make together.

🔗 Join our community: Google Developer Student Club - MIT and follow our LinkedIn page for the latest updates!

And then i started coding my solution within 20 mins . While dry running some edge cases were stuck and later did some modifications which passed that edge case too.

experiences.title: Google Interview Experience | Software Engineer University Graduate 2025
experiences.full_content:
The moment I saw the email from Google about my selection for the Software Engineer University Graduate 2025 hiring process, it felt surreal. I was on a bus, returning from college, when I checked my inbox and saw the mail. My heart raced with excitement as I read through the details. Google had asked me to confirm my interest by filling out a form and scheduling an interview. It was a dream come true—the kind of moment every aspiring software engineer hopes for.

Initial Steps: Setting the Stage

After filling out the form with my qualifications and preferred interview dates, I received confirmation for November 11, 2024. Google also scheduled a virtual briefing for all selected candidates on November 5, where we learned about the process: four technical rounds focused on problem-solving and coding skills.

I began preparing intensely right away. Over the next ten days, I sharpened my skills, focusing on the LeetCode Blind 75 problems—a resource I discovered through LinkedIn connections with experienced candidates. I also revisited concepts from Love Babbar’s DSA course, prioritizing topics like graphs and trees to prepare for any challenging question.

An Unexpected Twist

On the morning of November 11, I received an unexpected email: my interview had been canceled due to a scheduling conflict and rescheduled for November 21, 2024. While initially disappointed, I saw it as an opportunity to refine my preparation further. Despite some personal commitments that week, including a family function, I balanced my time to stay focused on coding practice and theoretical revisions.

The Interview Experience

At 3 PM on November 21, I logged in for my first technical round. The interviewer was friendly and began with an introduction. Soon, he presented a problem based on arrays and intervals. I explained two different approaches, analyzing their time and space complexities. The discussion went well, and we moved on to the coding task.

However, I made a minor mistake in my code. Despite a subtle hint from the interviewer, I couldn’t resolve it within the allotted time. The interview concluded with a chance for me to ask questions, which I used to express genuine interest in the role.

The Outcome: A Bitter Disappointment

Later that evening, I received an email informing me I wouldn’t be moving forward in the process. It was disheartening to see my Google journey end so soon. However, I chose to view it as a valuable learning experience. The setback highlighted the importance of effective time management and avoiding errors under pressure.

Reflection and Lessons Learned

While rejection stings, it also fuels determination. Here’s what I’ve taken away from this experience:

Practice under time constraints: I’ll focus more on hands-on coding practice within strict time limits.
Strengthen fundamentals: Topics like arrays, graphs, and trees will be revisited more thoroughly.
Learn from mistakes: I aim to approach future interviews with better composure and time management.
Setbacks are an inevitable part of any journey. They’re not the end but stepping stones toward growth and success. To anyone preparing for similar opportunities: stay consistent, keep learning, and never give up on your dreams. The road to success is rarely smooth, but perseverance always pays off.

experiences.title: Google Interview Experience SWE FTE ( On-Campus 2024 )
experiences.full_content:
Online Assessment Round

Duration - 60 minutes

Questions - 2 from a set of 8 Questions for the test happening PAN India. 6 Questions were medium, 2 were hard.

Round - 1: Technical Round (45 Minutes)

Q1: Given N friends, each friend remembers some subsequence of an array. Check if such an array exists, if yes, find any possible array.

friend[0] = {1, 4, 2}, friend[1] = {2, 5, 3}, friend[3] = {1, 2, 3}, friend[4] = {4, 2, 5, 6}

One possible array satisfying each condition: {1, 4, 2, 5, 3, 6}

Solution: This is a classical problem of Topological Sort. I explained BFS and DFS approaches for this and write code for both also. This was completed within 20-25 minutes. The interviewer was super impressed by the speed. The interviewer came with only 1 question, so she asked around 5-6 easy questions after this.

This interview ended within 35 minutes.

Round - 2: Technical + HR Round (60 Minutes)

Question 1: The farmer owns an N x M meter field and is facing financial challenges. He's considering selling most of the field but wants to keep a 3x3 section while conserving water usage. Each 1 x 1 plot needs a specific amount of water. Your task is to identify the optimal 3x3 slot for him, considering water efficiency.

(Given a NxM matrix, find the minimum sum of 3x3 sub-matrix.)

Example: Given matrix:

[

1,2,3,4,5,4,

3,1,2,1,0,4,

2,6,7,0,1,1,

4,6,7,0,0,1,

1,2,4,6,2,3,

2,7,9,8,1,5,

]

for the sub-matrix [ (row=1, coloumn=3) to (row=3, column=5)], the sum is 8 and this is the minimum 3x3 cells.

Solution : This is also a classical problem of prefix sums. I started with a prefix sum based solution. Interviewer asked me to optimise the code to O(1) space complexity. After this, he came up with a follow up question .

Question 2 : Consider a situation where you are given matrix sizes NxM, but some plots have a value of zero. Your task is to find the minimum 3x3 plot on this grid where all 9 plots have a non-zero value.
Solution : This is also a similar problem, where we just need to track the zeroes. I write code with time complexity = O(n  m) and space complexity = O(m).

Then, interviewer asked 3-4 general situation based questions. Interview ended in around 50 minutes.

Round - 3 : Technical + HR Round (60 Minutes)

Question : Consider a game called "The Odd One Out":  You're given a list of words, and you have to figure out which word is the "odd one out", or the least similar word.  For example, given "red, blue, green, cow, yellow", the odd one out is "cow", because it is an animal, not a color.

Write a function that given a list of words, determines which one is the odd one out.

You also have access to a universe of words, where each word comes with a set of words that are its attributes.

For example, "cow" has the following attributes: "animal, mammal, white, etc.".

cow - "animal, mammal, white, etc.".

table - "furniture, legs, brown"

kitten - "baby, cat, pet, white"

Input:-

table - "furniture, legs, brown, books"

bed -  "furniture, legs, brown"

chair - "furniture, legs, yellow"

study table - "furniture, legs, black, books, lamp, computer, paper"

Solution : This was a tricky question to understand, I was not getting how exactly odd one is to be filtered. Then, I discussed many examples with interviewer to get better understanding of question. Then got to know, function need to return that object, after removal of which, rest all objects has maximum number of common properties.

Initially, I came up with DSU based approach but it didn't worked. Then, I came to solution using prefix and suffix based approach. I used prefix and suffix array of set, ( let's say we are at index 'i', then prefix[i] will be a set which will contain all properties common in objects from index 0 to i, and suffix[i] will be a set which will contain all properties common in objects from index i to n-1. )

Then we iterate through each object, and check how many properties are common in all objects, if we remove 'i'th object by merging prefix[i-1] and suffix[i+1], the index where we get maximum size of this merge, will be our answer.

This approach was correct, I wrote code for the same, this took around 40 minutes. Then, interviewer asked 3-4 Googliness  questions.
This interview ended in around 55 minutes.

experiences.title: Google SWE Intern 2025 (Selected)
experiences.full_content:

Google opens this opportunity every year at the end of the second year. The earlier you apply, the sooner you get to know your application’s outcome. However, I was in the middle of my Amazon internship at that time and was waiting for the referral. Then, after getting referral I applied on 20th June on the last day of Application .

I was fully confident in myself that my profile would get shortlisted. At the time of applying my coding profile was:

Leetcode: 1500+ Ratings (Top 30% in Global) [400+ Qns Solved]

Codechef: 2 ⭐, Ratings of 1425

Telephonic Interview:

It was on 5th July 2024, I had completed my Amazon internship on 28th June, 2024 with a PPI and after that I was busy for my End sems of 4th Semester, I was in habit of Scrolling mails everyday and what I found, A mail from Google Recruiter for Telephonic interview. I booked the interview on same evening.

On that call, the recruiter introduced herself at first and then told me to introduce myself. Then, ask about my Internship experience about the contributions there , projects, tech-stack and coding profiles. Then, we discussed the language in which I am comfortable. Then, the recruiter asked if you were free this week or not, I requested for 15 days time as my end-sems were going on and then she agreed and told me tentative interview date 22nd July, 2024

I didn’t received any reply for 22nd July and literally was having no hope. But then on 7th Aug, I received mail that I will have 1st interview tomorrow(8th Aug).

Technical Interview 1:

Questions: 2 Questions with Code

Q1 (Medium): The interviewer shared me a link of Google interviewing doc and started with 1st problem. She wrote a single line problem statement with no testcases and told me to generate some edge cases for the problem. I thought for 2 mins, Generated some testcases, told my approach and time space complexities to the interviewer. She agreed and I coded out with code quality. Took around 30 mins in this problem.

Q2 (Medium - Hard): The interviewer shared another problem statement which seemed to be a DP ques. only 10 mins were left. I got the approach and explained with time and space complexities. She agreed and I started with recursion and optimized to memoization.

The interview ended with a 5 min discussion about culture at Google. Interview went well but I was nervous.

Preparation for Interview 2:

On the next day of 1st interview , I received an unexpected mail that I am shortlisted for 2nd Interview and it will be on 16th August,2024. I was having 1 week and prepared thoroughly Graphs, DP, Binary search, Trees and sliding window from Striver’s YT Playlist.

Technical Interview 2:

Questions: 2 Questions with Code

Q1 (Medium): The interviewer shared me a link of Google interviewing doc and started with 1st problem. He wrote a single line problem statement with 2 testcases and explained me problem statement thoroughly . It was a graph based problem. I thought for 2 mins, told my approach and time space complexities to the interviewer. He agreed and I coded out with code quality. Took around 20 mins in this problem.

Q2 (Medium — Hard): The interviewer asked a follow up question of the 1st PS. It was again a graph based problem. I told 2 approaches with time space complexities and he guided me to the best Time space complexity solution. I Coded it out.

Interviewer asked me why i used HashMap everywhere instead of Adjacency List , I replied because HashMap takes O(1) time and he seemed impressed. I was quiet confident about this interview and hoping for best.

Recruiter call for transcripts (28th Aug) :

My recruiter called me on 28th August,2024 around 7pm that I need to submit all my transcripts immediately by tonight and told that she will tell the final result tomorrow. I submitted and my heartbeat was very high, my parents and I was hoping for high🤞.

Recruiter call for Offer (29th Aug) :

Next Day around 2pm, I received call from an unknown number, put the call on speaker ,my mom and sister were listening. The call was of Google recruiter. She told me to guess what will be the result 😊, I said mam it was my 1st interview with Google and it went well and thanked her for supporting me throughout the process.

She told Dhruvi U got the Offer for Google SWE Intern 2025 Congratulations🎉and literally I was so happy and my mom thanked her on call.

experiences.title: Google Winter Intern Interview Experience
experiences.full_content:
I recently had the opportunity to interview for the Google Winter Intern position. While the outcome wasn’t in my favor, the journey was insightful and taught me a lot. Here’s a detailed recount of my experience:

Application Process

Applied: Submitted my application with a referral.
16th September 2024: Received an email from HR to schedule a telephonic round.
18th September 2024: HR interview focused on my resume and outlined the process: two technical rounds (45 minutes each), solely on Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA).

1st Technical Round – 30th September 2024

This round turned out to be one of the best interview experiences I’ve ever had.

Highlights:

Introduction: The session started with a quick introduction, setting a comfortable tone.
Problem Statement: A graph-based problem was presented. I asked clarifying questions before explaining my approach, which involved using graphs and a combination of data structures like maps of pairs and vectors.
Solution:Completed the initial solution within 25 minutes.
The interviewer then added special constraints and asked me to optimize further.
Used a priority queue to efficiently handle the constraints and completed the task in 35 minutes.

Discussion: We spent the remaining time chatting about college life and placements.
Outcome: Positive feedback was confirmed by HR on 1st October 2024.

2nd Technical Round – 7th October 2024

The second round was equally challenging and tested my problem-solving abilities under pressure.

Highlights:

Problem Statement: The interviewer presented a problem and asked me to explain my approach.
Solution:Initially solved it using Dynamic Programming (DP), but the interviewer asked for further optimization.
After a brief pause to think, I proposed a solution using maps and optimized the time and space complexity to O(n).
With 13–14 minutes remaining, the interviewer gave me a follow-up question with minor changes, which I quickly solved and coded.

Final Discussion: I asked her about Google’s work culture and the tech stack they use.

Outcome

After a long wait and multiple follow-ups, I received an update on 14th November 2024 that my application would not be moving forward.

Reflections

Although the result was disappointing, this experience taught me invaluable lessons about preparation, adaptability, and staying calm under pressure. The technical rounds emphasized not just solving problems but also optimizing and clearly explaining solutions.

experiences.title: HCL Tech Interview Experience | HCL Tech Bee Program
experiences.full_content:
In 2022, I found myself at a crossroads, faced with an opportunity that could shape my career—the HCL Tech Bee program. The program promised one year of training, an on-the-job opportunity at HCL, and the chance to pursue higher education through EAPCET counseling. It seemed perfect, except for one major hurdle: the eligibility criteria required a minimum of 60% in MPC (Maths, Physics, and Chemistry).

The Challenge of Eligibility

Due to the pandemic (2020–2022), our first-year intermediate exams were canceled, and students were given passing marks. To improve scores, students could attempt a "betterment" exam, but I contracted COVID-19 and was hospitalized, leaving me with borderline results—just 57% in MPC. My low marks in Mathematics were particularly disappointing.

When I shared my decision to apply for the program with my parents, they were furious.

"How could you end up with just 57%? You were such a bright student in school!"

Their disappointment weighed heavily on me, and the situation felt like a matter of life and death. Despite their anger and my own doubts, I decided to take a chance.

The Exam

The first step in the application process was a qualifying exam. On test day, I gave it my all and felt confident about my performance. An examiner even reassured me: "If you pass, you’ll receive an email for an interview."

Days passed, but no email arrived. My parents’ frustration grew.

"You weren’t even eligible to begin with. Why did you even try?"

Their words stung deeply, and I began to doubt myself. One night, overwhelmed with emotions, I broke down, thinking maybe my 57% was the reason for my failures.

Out of desperation, I checked my email again. To my shock, I realized I had missed my interview invite! My heart sank—it felt like the end of the road.

The Call That Changed Everything

Determined not to give up, I nervously called the examiner, explaining my mistake.

"I missed the interview invite in my email. Is there any chance I can still attend?"

After a pause, the examiner said,

"Let me see what I can do. I’ll reschedule it for you, but this is your last chance. Don’t mess it up."

I couldn’t believe my luck. I thanked him profusely and promised to make the most of this opportunity.

The Interview

On the interview day, I double-checked everything to ensure no mistakes. The call began with the interviewer asking:

"Tell us a little about yourself."

I shared my story—my schooling, struggles during the pandemic, and aspirations.

"What do you want to be in the future?"

I want to work in tech, creating solutions that can help people in their everyday lives through HCL," I replied.

The next question caught me off guard:

"What’s your favorite book?"

I smiled and said, "Harry Potter."

The interviewer responded, "Great choice! Now, open a notebook and write 100 words about the book. We’ll be watching."

The pressure was intense, but I stayed calm, writing with focus and clarity. After submitting my work, the examiner said:

"You have an incredible way with words. Your confidence and fluent English are remarkable."

I was stunned and proud.

The Selection

Two days later, I received the news—I had been selected! My parents, though initially frustrated, were now ecstatic.

We were invited to the HCL headquarters in Vijayawada to discuss the curriculum:

Six months of online training followed by six months of offline training.
A fee of ₹1 lakh for the program, which included laptops for the course.
Despite the cost, I was thrilled to embark on this new journey.

A Twist of Fate

Just two days after the visit to Vijayawada, my EAPCET counseling results were announced. To my delight, I secured a CSE seat at ANITS, a prestigious college in Visakhapatnam.

After careful consideration, I chose to prioritize my studies over the HCL Tech Bee program.

When I informed the examiner of my decision, he expressed disappointment:
"I had great expectations for you. You should have informed me sooner."

Hearing his words, I felt a pang of regret for leaving the program after all the effort.

Reflection

Looking back, my experience with the HCL Tech Bee program taught me the importance of perseverance, self-confidence, and taking chances—even when the odds aren’t in your favor.

Though I ultimately chose a different path, the journey remains a pivotal moment in my life. It reminded me that setbacks are not the end but opportunities to grow stronger.

To anyone facing challenges, remember: take the chance, believe in yourself, and never give up. You never know how far it might take you.

Managerial

what are joins and explain all types of joins

experiences.full_content:
I recently went through the selection process for the Graduate Engineer Trainee (GET) role at HCLTech, and I’m excited to share my journey. The eligibility criteria required 70% throughout academics with no backlogs. The process consisted of four rounds: an online assessment, HR screening, a technical interview, and an HR interview.

1. Online Assessment

The first step was an online test comprising 75 questions to be completed within 90 minutes. The test was divided into several sections:

Coding-Based Exercises
Technical MCQ Key Topics (DBMS, OOPS, CN, ST, OS)
Logical, Verbal, and Quantitative Reasoning
Analytical and Critical Reasoning

2. HR Screening

experiences.full_content:
The requirement process of Hexaware Technologies Ltd. at our college Knowledge Institute of Technology. We got the official notification from our college and the whole process was taken on the Superset Platform. My journey with Hexaware started on the 13th of August 2024 when our college sent the notification of Hexaware and the eligible list of Students for Hexaware Technologies. I have shared my experience and key takeaways.

I was one of the eligible person at Hexaware Technologies.

Eligibility criteria for Hexaware is given below:

Graduating candidates should be from the BE/B Tech /MCA.
Candidates should be from any of the branches CSE/IT/ECE/EEE/ETC/EIE/ICE and circuit branches.
Mechanical and Civil allied branches are not eligible.
Passing year: 2025
Aggregate till last announced results: 60% or 6.0 CGPA throughout 10th, 12th and UG/PG.
Candidates should not have an active backlog.
Candidates having more than 1 year of education gap/ break are detained in their graduation is not eligible.

They conducted 5 rounds of interview (3 rounds for GET + 2 rounds for PGET) which are given below:

Round 1: Online Aptitude + Domain test (Pseudocode + Computer Fundamentals)
Round 2: Group Discussions
Round 3: HR Discussions
Round 4: Coding assessment
Round 5: EC Interview
I will tell the each round round in the detail below.

Round 1 : Online Aptitude + Domain Test (90 mins):

I had the first round on 29.08.2024 where online aptitude and Domain test. I took the test on Superset platform in association Cocubes platform. In the online aptitude we had the all the questions combination of Quants, Logical reasoning and English. In the Quants the question difficulty was Easy to moderate level some of question was the given as the direct formula application here. Pseudocode was very simple logic and some questions were the Bit Manipulation based questions was also asked and we can able to manage this by basic knowledge of the Bit Manipulation.

In our college around 430 students were eligible and 242 was selected and I was the one of them.

Round 2: Group Discussion

Hexaware team visited our college on 10.09.2024 for conducting the group discussion in our college. There were around the 16 group for the with 15 to 16 members each. The topic of the GD is based upon the HR's decision. For me my HR was very friendly where he has asked to choose our own topics.
Note: The topic was both the General and technical.

Some of the topics are listed below which were asked in our college GD:

Impact of AI in employements (This was asked for me).
Is the Deadline is good or not for the enhancing the productivity.
Hard work vs Smart work.
City Life vs Village Life.
In our college from 242 students they selected around 75 students were selected for HR Interview. I was one of them.

Round 3: HR Discussion

I got a mail from hexaware that my interview was scheduled on 16th September 2024 which was on online. They took the HR discussion on the superset platform it was around 10 -20 mins for me. The HR was very friendly and asked some of the basic questions. Some questions asked are given below:

Introduce yourself.
Are you willing to relocate?
Tell about the company.
Where you will be in 5 years from now?
Do you know about the service agreement?
This was the end of GET role interview where among 75 students 43 students were offered for the GET role. I also offered for the GET role initially.

Round 4: Coding assessment (40mins)

I had the coding assessment 21.10.2024. I had  the coding assessment on Superset platform in the association of Cocubes. They provided to choose any language out of C/C++/Java/Python. We can able to choose our convenient language. I preferred Java to code since I am good at it. There were 2 questions which was easy to medium level. Out of 43 candidates 24 students were selected for this round.

Question asked for me is given below:

1. Odd or even Sequence Check.

A sequence is only deemed exceptional if it does not contain any neighboring numbers that together comprise either both odd or even integers. You are given T test cases, and an array array of size N is handed to you for each test case. Each test case should output "YES" if the sequence is unique, and "NO" otherwise.

Input :

1 4 1 4 2 8

Output:

True

2.  Find total of array if minimum number and its adjacent number is removed.

You are presented with an array of N numbers. The number itself and its surrounding elements are removed each time the array's minimal value is chosen. Until the array is completely empty of integers, this operation is repeated. It is your responsibility to determine and output the sum of the minimal numbers being removed from the array.

Input:

7 6 4 9 10 34 56 54

Output

68

In our college 24 attended and 13 students were selected for the next round of EC interview. I was one of them.

Round 5: EC Interview

I had my EC interview on 24.12.2024. The EC interview means effective communication interview where I had the both the general and the technical questions. For me they took 25 mins to complete the whole interview process. The interview was scheduled in the superset platform. Some of the questions asked are given below.

About the final year project.
Questions asked from the coding assessment.
About the family.
About the projects.
After this interview out of 13 students 7 got the offer of PGET. I was one of them.
